subtopic: DISPOSAL OF SEIZED U.S. CIGARETTES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISPOSAL OF SEIZED U.S. CIGARETTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct to the Minister of National Revenue two questions of which I

have given notice. What is being done with the large quantities of United States cigarettes that are being seized by customs officials and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police? Are they being allowed to displace Canadian cigarettes for sale in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: DISPOSAL OF SEIZED U.S. CIGARETTES
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for having given me notice of his questions. Cigarettes that are seized are first put in what is known as the king's warehouse. They are afterward distributed to veteran hospitals throughout the country. The practice formerly followed was to destroy such cigarettes. This distribution is made by officials of the Department of National Revenue, customs and excise branch, who in practically all instances are veterans. They visit the hospitals and make a personal distribution.
The hon. member asked also whether the cigarettes are allowed to displace Canadian-made cigarettes for sale in Canada. The broad answer to that would be "no". They do not enter into competition except in so far as the recipients in veterans hospitals would probably buy Canadian made cigarettes if they did not get the ones which have been seized. They are not in competition with them on the open market.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last evening of this debate when I was speaking I was about to read from United States fishery products report No. 224, to be found in the bulletin of the fisheries council of Canada of November 30 1951. This reads:
The outlook for increased fish production appears to be promising, for the FAO study reports that many countries are adding, or planning to add. mechanized craft to the fishing fleets to fish in areas farther from port and save on travel time. Moreover, the report adds, improvements in fishing gear and equipment are being made in many underdeveloped as well as developed countries.
I am aware that at the present time a joint committee is sitting in Newfoundland under the chairmanship of Chief Justice Sir Albert Walsh, a man who knows the customs of the

The Address-Mr. Adamson country and who for several years was a member of the commission of government. The fishermen of Newfoundland will be looking forward to the contents of this report when it appears, but I do want to point out to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) that if our interest in the fisheries is allowed to lag, and if we allow our fisheries to decline, as appears to be the policy of the provincial government, other nations more vigorous than ours will step in and take our rightful place as the greatest fishing country in the world.
Today is the fiftieth anniversary of the reception by Marconi, the inventor of wireless telegraphy, of the first transatlantic message. Fifty years ago in Cabot tower on Signal hill, above the narrows of St. John's harbour, a copper wire suspended from a kite picked up a signal transmitted from Cornwall, thus justifying the confidence of Marconi in his discovery and inventions. The untold benefits mankind has derived as other scientists have improved upon Marconi's invention justify our grateful commemoration of the astonishing event that occurred just half a century ago.
I have only one other thing to say and that is to compliment the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) upon the solicitude that he showed the other day when he referred to the Canadian sisters who have been victims of the Chinese communists. 1 should like to draw to the attention of the house an article that appeared in La Presse yesterday, which reads:
(Translation):
Persecutions have cut down by two-thirds the number of missionaries in China.
As a result of the efforts of Chinese communists to drive the Catholic church out of China, the number of missionaries has fallen from 5,000 to 1,879. Every day, other missionaries are being expelled, or jailed prior to deportation. Most Protestant missionaries, never as numerous as Catholic missionaries, have left China. It is not known how many have remained.
According to the last survey, there were 142 foreign Catholic missionaries in the prisons of China and there are probably twice that number being kept under close watch in their homes.
Among Catholic missionaries jailed by the communists, are the following Canadians:
Mgr. Cuthbert O'Gara, of Ottawa: Rev. Arsine Mullin, O.F.M., of Montreal; Rev. Didace Arcand, O.F.M., of Three Rivers . . .
... and many other priests and nuns from Canada.

I should like also to refer to an article which appeared in The Sign of November, 1951, which reads:
Countless martyrs have shed their blood. Today it is "dry martyrdom." A long slow process calculated to reach into a man's inmost being and dry up all spirit of resistance or desire to acknowledge

anything but what is forced upon him. A slow but definitely effective process the horrors of which are beyond the imagination of those who have not fallen victims, a deadly inhuman diabolic process that reached its almost perfect form in the Mindszenty case.
Hunan-
A province in China.
-is now the training ground for this modern Soviet type of oppression and destruction. Bishop O'Gara-
Who is well known in Ottawa.
-is in prison, his priests under constant threat, his diocese in the hands of renegades, his faithful dreading each moment of the day and night. God be with them.
How can we feel happy when these people are facing martyrdom? All Canadians have a right to expect that their government will do everything possible to protect their lives and bring about the release of these heroic men and women.

I do
not wish to prolong this debate an instant longer than is absolutely necessary, but I wish to refer once again to the remarks the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made in this house concerning cases of dismissal for security reasons. I still believe, Mr. Speaker, that some machinery must be set up whereby a man who is considered a poor security risk has the opportunity of hearing the case against him. I do not believe that this requires any breach of security, and I am convinced that it can be done without in any way disclosing the necessarily secret methods employed by the security forces of the country. Notwithstanding the genuine feelings of the Prime Minister concerning these cases, and the fears of allowing security material to be compromised, I feel that we in this house, as the custodians of the freedom of the individual, cannot permit these dismissals to continue without recourse to any appeal.
I thank the Prime Minister for the objective way in which he dealt with my submissions in this case. I feel that the present system is unsatisfactory, and I do suggest that it is dangerous to the genuine security and freedom of this peace-loving country.

I believe that the representa-

I believe that the officials of the tea bureau are not fooling the citizens of Ottawa in sending out a report of that kind. First of all, it must be realized that anyone practising these tea bag tricks would not admit to anyone that such was the case. They are not pulling the wool over the eyes of these victims of the tea bag tricks. I am not retracting one word of the complaint I made a week ago. The practice is injurious to the health of the people in this and other cities, and I feel that the publicity that has been given to it will prevent offenders from continuing the practice.

Mr. Speaker, while the government is trying to make up its mind whether it should carry out the suggestion and accept the vote as one of want of confidence, there is another matter that I want to bring to the attention of the house. I am quite sure that members on the opposition side of the house will appreciate the fact that during the present session, with no budget and no estimates, the throne speech is the one opportunity when members may deal with subjects of general interest to the country. I am confident that members on the Liberal side of the house, since they were quite ready to spend almost an entire day debating a meaningless amendment to the amendment so that Liberals would not find it inconvenient to vote against the amendment, will bear with me for a few moments on this question. I want to discuss a statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) when speaking to the house on October 25. At that time he was introducing the resolution preceding the old age security bill, and at page 381 of Hansard he said:
As my colleagues and I have so frequently emphasized in the years since 1945, the broad social objectives then outlined by the federal government have constantly remained in the forefront of its thinking and planning.
I want to bring to the attention of the house what some of these broad social objectives were which were proposed, by the government in 1945. One of great interest to the country was a nationally based and nation-wide social security program which included among other things social and health insurance together with hospitalization. I want to quote-and I shall not be long-from the proposals made in 1945. At page 28 there is the following:
Although great progress has been made in Canada during the first half of this century, there still remains a tremendous job to be done in improving the national health and in extending the benefits of modern science and medical care to all parts of the nation and all sections of the population.
Then I want to read another quotation from page 28. This is the Liberal government speaking in 1945. It reads:
Under our present system, for the man who can afford to pay, the cost of ill health falls at the very moment when his earning capacity is cut off. The cost of treatment and cure for the individual who cannot afford to pay is borne to a considerable degree through the benefactions of well to do members of the community and the generosity of doctors who give so freely of their time and skill, and more and more by the provincial governments and municipalities. In spite of these efforts desirable treatment is still not obtained in many cases. While

much of the cost of illness is thus hidden^ it can only come out of the total productive capacity of the country. The advantages of a broader provision of health services on a more equitable basis are obvious.	.
That was in the year 1945. Then there is another choice statement, and I quote it because the spokesmen for the government who prepared these proposals put the sentiments I want to express today in words that are as good as any that I could use. They said:
To remove disparities in standards of health services in different parts of Canada, to avoid the risks of sudden heavy expenditures, and distribute health costs more widely and equitably, and above all to obtain the benefits of better health for the great majority of our people, these are the objects of the proposals which the federal government is now making with respect to health insurance for all, and increased public health services assisted by federal grants.
The government, or at least the Liberal party, has apparently been interested in health insurance for a long time. We find that health insurance first found itself in the election manifesto of the Liberal party back in 1919, only thirty-two years ago. I suppose thirty-two years is not much in the lifetime of a political party and possibly the Liberals consider that thirty-two years is really not sufficient time for them to begin to implement their election manifesto promises.
We are now in 1951, thirty-two years since the Liberals first adopted the principle of health insurance as an election program, as an election promise. We are back now, probably not to where we were thirty-two years ago but certainly to where we were in 1941 or 1942. The government went much further than to just offer these pious proposals for health insurance; in 1945 the government actually spelled out these proposals and gave them to us in considerable detail. On page 29 of their proposals they stated:
Health insurance has been widely adopted because it is regarded as the best means of meeting and of distributing fairly the costs of illness and, in conjunction with preventive services, of improving the general health of the nation. Specifically:
(1)	Health insurance enables the cost of illness to be prepaid, so that by paying regular sums when they are well people are able to meet the costs of illness when they are ill without being financially crippled.
(2)	Health insurance not only enables individuals to prepay their medical costs, but does this in such a way as to secure a wide pooling of risks and distribution of costs in much the same manner as any other form of insurance.
(3)	The provision of funds by all persons within a large area makes it possible for hospital and medical services to people in that area to be planned and administered more efficiently and economically than could be done by any other method.

(4)	The provision of better facilities for treatment and advice also operates to reduce the total incidence of disease and preventable death. Health insurance must be accompanied by adequate public health measures of a preventive character, but health insurance itself also provides important preventive benefits.
(5)	Health insurance permits the steady extension of health services into areas not previously covered, and the rapid application everywhere of new methods and services as they are discovered and developed.
In that language the government set forth back in 1945 most definitely its proposal of a health insurance program. Prior to 1945 th^y had done some spade work. In 1941 the then minister of pensions and national health had called a meeting of health authorities and persons interested in public welfare. It will be noted that that meeting was called only twenty-two years after the Liberals first adopted health insurance into the election manifesto. In twenty-two years' time they managed to get around to the point where the minister was calling a meeting.
In 1942 the government appointed an advisory committee on this matter. In 1943 a House of Commons committee was set up, and in that year the advisory committee reported to the House of Commons committee and presented a draft bill in which all the details were worked out. I recall the election which followed the presentation of that draft bill. It was pretty generally understood throughout the country that all that was needed to have that bill become legislation was to elect the Liberal party. That was the general appeal made by the Liberal party in that year. In 1944 a conference was called at Ottawa of representatives of all the provinces. Various views were put forth, and in that connection the proposals were as follows:
In May, 1944, a conference was held at Ottawa which was attended by representatives of all the provinces. The discussion principally turned on the estimated cost of the services contemplated under the draft health insurance bill and on the manner of meeting this cost. Views were put forward by several provinces which appeared to have the support of most if not all of the provinces. These indicated their strong desire that health insurance should be proceeded with by stages and that any scheme adopted should be flexible enough to permit the provinces to build on the varying services in each province.
In the throne speeches of 1944 and 1945 health insurance was included as part of the Liberal policy. That was one of the objectives that the Liberal party held out to the Canadian public just on the eve of the 1945 elections. Four definite proposals on the subject of health insurance were set out by the government in 1945. The scheme was to include a grant for planning and organization; it was to include health insurance; it
The Address^Mr. Noseivorthy was to include health grants; and it was to include federal assistance in the construction of hospitals. The proposed federal contribution was as follows:
(i)	a basic grant of one-fifth of the estimated cost of each service as shown on the table which follows as from time to time revised by agreement, and
(ii)	one-half the additional actual cost incurred by each provincial government of providing each benefit, provided that the total federal contribution does not exceed the amount stated in the table for each service, or maximum of $12.96 per person, when the complete program is in operation.
That was the financial basis upon which the program was to progress. Among other help that was to be granted, I am particularly interested in the reference to financial assistance in the construction of hospitals. The proposal stated:
To make a hospital extension program less burdensome to the provincial governments and to local communities, it is proposed that the federal government should provide loans to the provincial governments entering health insurance agreements, and through provincial governments to municipalities and other organizations, for necessary expansion of hospital facilities, at a rate of interest equal to or only slightly above the cost of such loans to the dominion. . .
That was to be one of the ways in which the government was to make its contribution towards the building of hospitals. There were to be loans from the government, and there were to be the basic amounts for health insurance grants for various types of assistance. We are now in 1951, and where are we with health insurance? We are back in 1942 or a little farther back than 1942. In 1942 we did have a committee, but in 1951 we have only the promise of a committee which is to be set up at the next session. Apparently the government's policy concerning this matter underwent a change in 1948, and Mr. King's announcement of the new policy on May 14 included no provision whatever for health insurance. Since then there has been no indication that the government is seriously considering the implementation of that 32-year-old promise to the Canadian people.
There can be no reasonable argument for delaying the implementation of that program. The government cannot say that these proposals were made, and were subject to agreement with the provinces. It was clearly set out that these proposals were flexible, and that any province could enter into an agreement to put into effect any part of this program that it was felt it could do at that time. The proposals were flexible enough to permit any province that wanted to institute health insurance to enter into an agreement with the federal government whereby it would get the federal aid set out

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy in these proposals for the implementation of health insurance. Other countries, probably less fortunate than Canada, have instituted health insurance since 1945.
I should like to read briefly from an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star under date of December 8, 1951. I am quite sure that Liberals will listen to any editorial appearing in a paper which is so devoted to the Liberal party and the Liberal cause.

speechtext:
The Star mentions an address made by Dr. Fraser Brockington of Manchester university on the subject of health insurance and social medicine. In summarizing that address the Star has this to say:
The British national health scheme is In the third year of its operation.
In other words, Great Britain, with all her handicaps, with the aftermath of war and all her financial problems since 1945, has been able to institute an over-all health insurance program similar to that which this government proposed in 1945, but which we in Canada have not been able to implement. The editorial continues:
It has already reduced the backlog of neglected health among a large portion of the population, and improved the efficiency of hospitals and other facilities. It has made possible for people in outlying areas to obtain the services of specialists where they were not easily available before. The nursing supply has been increased, as well as hospital beds. Maternity and child welfare services, home nursing and domestic aid have been extended. A national deafness service is a new addition through which hearing aids are being provided at the rate of 6,000 a month, most of them to elderly people who could not afford them in the past.
Perhaps the most important benefit of the national health service is psychological. It has removed from the entire population the fear of sickness. It has eliminated the financial barrier to medical care. The service is especially appreciated by the middle classes, individuals and families whose income ranges between $2,000 and $5,000 a year. To these groups, sickness often brings calamitous burdens of debt. The health service guarantees protection to them and many others. No one in Britain now becomes shackled by debts for surgical operation, childbirth or hospitalization for a long, chronic ailment.
Then-, this is interesting:
The British national health service is mostly financed by general taxation. About a ninth of the cost is covered by contributions from employees and employers. An employed man (single or married) pays about 10 cents a week; a woman pays 7i cents and an employer 1-8 cents. They contribute also as direct or indirect taxpayers. And everyone, without distinction on any ground, is entitled to whatever medical or hospital services are required for cure and prevention of sickness.
There is one other point brought out in this editorial that is interesting to Canadians

in general. Dr. Brockington refers to the British national health service as social medicine. He says:
-it is "social medicine," in that all essential health facilities are being extended to everyone on a cooperative basis, with due respect to the rights of those who give and those who receive the service. Doctors, dentists, pharmacists, etc., are not salaried employees of the state . . .
I wanted to point out that Great Britain, with all the difficulties, turmoil and aftermath of the war, was able to embark upon a social and health insurance program such as outlined there. We in this country are under a Liberal government that professes to believe in such a program, that has been promising such a program to the Canadian people for over thirty years, and that at one time reached the point of having a draft bill ready, which bill was held out to the Canadian public at election time when the appeal was made that all that was necessary to have the bill placed on the statute books was the election of the Liberal party. I might add that in recent months the Liberals in Ontario particularly have appeared to be quite interested in health insurance and hospitalization. Some cabinet ministers from this government went into Ontario in support of that program during the campaign. Did the minister say no?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitated a moment lest the Minister of National Health and Welfare wished to comment on this further amendment. I hope he will do so even yet. A few words from him would be quite sufficient, if they are the right words. I can assure you, sir, and the house that what I have to say at this point will be brief.
I want to indicate that, in my view, the subject matter of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) is one of the most important questions facing this country at the present time. It is a matter of extreme concern to all our people. We are slowly but surely making some headway in the field of social legislation, particularly in that we are getting rid of the means test with respect to the old age pension for those 70 and over and in that we are getting a pension started at age 65.
There are other improvements necessary in that legislation, principally an increase in the amount. But, as I have pointed out on a number of occasions, it is becoming extremely important that we bring in along with our old age legislation some forward steps in the field of health. I need not rehearse the story that has been given by my colleague with respect to the promises that have been made by this government across the years but which are not measured up to by actual performance. It certainly is a fact that our people across this country are interested in this whole problem of health and need some attention to be given to it. The wording of the amendment proposed by my colleague
The Address-Mr. Knowles pin-points what is really needed, namely a national health plan, including hospitalization, medical care and health insurance.
There are various appropriate announcements that the Minister of National Health and Welfare could make at this time. I hope that the least he will do is to confirm the promise he made last June to the effect that at the 1952 session of parliament there will be a special parliamentary committee to go into this question. As he knows, ever since the work of the special parliamentary committee on old age security some of us have been urging that a further committee be set up; and during debates on this matter last June the minister indicated that we would have such a committee at the next session of parliament. I hope that the minister today will confirm that promise. I urge further that that committee be set up just as early as possible in the session that will start some time in the first part of 1952.
There is just one other comment that I want to make while I am on my feet, and it relates to a copy of a sessional paper which was tabled yesterday but which reached me just this morning. It is sessional paper No. 86-B which was tabled by the minister's parliamentary assistant, giving the answers to questions of mine having to do with requests from the provinces for grants for research purposes under the federal health grants program. This sessional paper sets out requests for grants for research purposes which have been turned down by the Department of National Health and Welfare. I want to register my protest against the action of the department or of the minister, or whoever is responsible, for turning down some of these requests. I think that action shows an indefensible lack of interest in some extremely important matters. For example, according to this sessional paper, the Newfoundland provincial government asked for assistance for:
A complete survey of the provincial hospitals which would improve their management and business procedures, under the terms of the general public health grant.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I know of a lot of things on which money is being spent which are a lot less important than a survey of the provincial hospitals of any province-in this case it was Newfoundland-with the hope of improving their management and procedures.
Then there was a request from Quebec for research into a certain aspect of arteriosclerosis, to be carried out at the pathological institute, McGill university, and at the Royal Victoria hospital in Montreal. We know how excellent is the work done at these institutions. I suggest that the failure to grant the money for that research project is something that we

The Address

Mr. Knowles should protest. Similarly, there was a request for money for research into the effects of electrical and chemical stimuli at the neuromuscular junction, to be carried out by the department of physiology, McGill university. There are a number of other requests such as that from outstanding centres of medicine across the country.
Then here is one that came from Ontario, and frankly, when I look at it, I am amazed that the government turned this down, unless they were afraid of the results. Just listen to this. It is a request from the Ontario provincial government for assistance for a research project on:
A housing and health survey in St. Thomas and district to discover the relationship, if any, between substandard housing and adult and child health.
I think that is definitely something that we should have research on, Mr. Speaker, namely the relationship between substandard housing and the health of our people. I think the government of Ontario is to be commended for proposing such a research project. I think that this government is to be condemned for turning down a project of that kind. There are others-I am not going to read them all-but there is one more I want to draw special attention to, and I am particularly disturbed that this request was refused. It was from the government of Saskatchewan. I am reading from the sessional paper that was tabled here yesterday. The request was for money for research on this subject:
An administrative analysis of health insurance plans operating in Canada with emphasis on the patterns of administration emerging in this new field of health service.
I do not know all the details, but I believe that Saskatchewan indicated it was possible to get financial assistance from other sources as well, if they could get some assistance from the federal government for this, and it does seem to me that it would have been a very valuable piece of research.
The federal government wants us to believe that it has some interest in the question of health insurance. We vote money every year in the estimates for health insurance studies. It took considerable effort on our part for quite a while to get the government to spend that money for that purpose, but they are spending money on health insurance studies. They have a director of health insurance studies, although he does have other work as well. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has given further evidence of at least some interest in the question of health insurance by his announcement that we are to have a special parliamentary committee on this subject next year. If that is so, it seems to me it would have been an excellent

idea to have a piece of research such as this carried on and perhaps completed before that committee is set up.
I do not know how wide it was intended that this survey be made, but it sounds as though the government of Saskatchewan was interested in an objective survey of the administration of health insurance plans operating in Canada in all the various parts of this country.
If the government is sincere in its interest in health insurance, sincere to the point of being willing to establish a parliamentary committee at the next session, I certainly think it should not have turned down that request. The amounts of money involved in these various research projects that are covered in this sessional paper 86-B I am sure would be only a drop in the bucket compared with the federal government expenditures at the present time, and I hope that the minister will reconsider his decision against these research grants. I feel that all of those that I have indicated-and perhaps the rest of them in this sessional paper- should have been made. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the minister will indicate that it is the intention to set up that special committee as early as possible at the next session of parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the question is put I should like to say just a word about the amendment, because I would not like to vote on it without making our position very clear. I must begin by saying that I am absolutely opposed to the amendment, not because I do not want to see our people throughout Canada have the advantage of any health measures which it is possible to extend to them, but I object very strongly to having these things all centralized in the federal government; I object strongly to having our people mollycoddled constantly and forced into becoming wards of a superstate.
I do not find it possible often to come to the assistance of the government, but when I do I like to make my position very clear. I think that the federal government has set about this whole business of health measures on a very wide program. I think they have done well, and I want to pay that tribute to them. They have done an outstanding job in the field of health, but they have had the good sense to work in close co-operation with the provincial governments in order to see to it that whatever assistance could be granted from the federal government to the authorities who are supposed to be looking after the health of the people-that is, the provincial and municipal governments-is

extended to them. I like a great many of the things that have been done by the department of health here. I could speak at length, but I do not intend to. I could enumerate the fine things that they have done to assist the provinces in their schemes for health insurance.
I would like to see more educational work done. There could be considerably more research, and perhaps more investigational projects. There certainly could be more education to assist our people to understand what it is that makes them sick, and to help them to follow a manner of living that will keep them well. I object to any national scheme that places a burden of taxation upon all the people to treat, we will say, a very large section of the population that will not do anything to keep themselves well. I do not think that is right. It is high time that we began to understand that until individuals in our country take advantage of the information that is available and educate themselves in nutrition and other health measures to the point where they will do their utmost to keep themselves out of hospital, until that time comes it is not wise to talk about taxing the daylight out of the rest for the sake of giving these others hospitalization and medical assistance.
When I say that, Mr. Speaker, I recognize that there are many people who could not do any more for themselves. I realize that. I realize, too, that there are many people who have no access to hospitalization or to doctors, because they cannot afford it. Certainly these are legitimate cases and there should be some way of helping them; but the best way to do it is to have the responsibilities placed upon the government nearest to them, and that is their municipal and provincial governments.
In our province of Alberta we have recognized the necessity of giving aid to our people as far as we possibly can, and that without taxing them to death. In the first place we decided years ago there were certain diseases that will strike members of families and will require long and costly treatment. Such diseases are likely to impoverish those families, and to render them homeless.
As a government we decided some years ago that it was our duty to step in and to assist in such cases. So we, as a government, took over the complete cost of poliomyelitis cases, and the after-training of individuals stricken with that disease, so that they could be fitted to earn something for themselves later on when their condition improved. We took over the full cost of the
The Address-Mr. Low treatment of cancer cases. We recognized also that, to cut down so far as possible the high rate of infant mortality, we should extend maternity hospitalization . of all expectant mothers, and do it at the expense of the government. That has been done. It has been going on very well for years. As a result, our infant mortality rate in Alberta has become very low.
Then, very early in the game we took over the full cost of the treatment of tuberculosis and, so long as necessary, the hospitalization incidental thereto. By taking these burdens off individuals the government has made it possible for families to get along, and has prevented their becoming impoverished through heavy medical costs.
We believe that in Alberta we have gone a long way in connection with hospitalization. We have now a scheme based upon careful and close co-operation between the provincial government and municipal authorities, and with the assistance of the federal government granted some years ago under a hospitalization scheme whereby individuals throughout the province can receive hospitalization for a dollar a day.
We felt it was wise to leave something to the individual. I do not believe it is good to give them everything. We felt in Alberta that a dollar a day was at least a token payment that almost any person could afford. It has had the effect that in Alberta one does not find the hospitals filled with patients complaining of bellyaches and ingrown toenails. They do not go to the hospitals unless they really need hospital treatment.
As a result we feel that our people gradually, step by step, are getting the kind of health assistance and health insurance they need. I believe it is wiser by far to work out schemes whereby the federal government will grant assistance through grants in aid so as, if possible, to equalize opportunities in respect of health facilities in all the provinces. We have felt it wise for the federal government to continue its investigational and research projects, and to make the results known to the people of Canada. This government should go as far as it can in assisting the provinces to inform the people about nutritional services and health measures of all kinds, so that people eventually will learn how to keep themselves well and out of the hospitals, as well as free from the necessity for medical care.
I wish to make it abundantly clear that we Social Crediters are favourable to every possible measure of assistance for our people in the field of health; but we strongly object to centralizing this in the federal government. Let us see to it that the fullest possible

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis measure of co-operation is built up between the federal government, the provincial governments and municipal governments. Let us see to it that we leave something to the individual. The only way in the world we can ever maintain a spirit of independence is to do something of that kind. So I say that until some such thing as we have been doing in Alberta can be conceived on a national scale, I must oppose the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure members that I rise to speak on this question with great reluctance, not because I am not interested in the subject matter of the amendment but like many other members of the house I hope to spend Christmas at home and I do not wish to hold up the house. I would not have spoken at all if it were not for certain remarks made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). That is one excuse, and if another is necessary, I have spoken very little in the house during the present session. I do not suppose I should ask credit for that because I feel I should have expressed my opinions more often. In this matter I suppose I feel like most people as they approach old age, namely, that the things they regret are
[Mr. Low.)

not the things they have done but the things they have not done. The amendment before the house reads:
This house further regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to make provision for a national health plan, including hospitalization, medical care and health insurance.
When the hon. member for Peace River spoke he gave the impression that the effect of the amendment would be to place all health matters under the control of the national government. Surely no member of this house believes that that is the purpose of the amendment, and least of all a member as intelligent as the hon. member for Peace River. All I want to do is to show that nothing more is included in the amendment than has been included in government statements in the house and in government documents over the last ten years. I have in my hand a book printed under the authority of the Department of Trade and Commerce, dominion bureau of statistics, health and welfare division. Its title is, "Health Reference Book, 1948." I should like to read briefly from the introduction on page 9 as follows:
Government activities directed toward improving Canadian health standards include a broad range of services carried out by dominion, provincial and municipal authorities. Within the Canadian federal system, the principal responsibility for health administration-
Note that it is not all responsibility but the principal responsibility.
-rests with provincial governments, the actual provision of service usually being shared with local authorities. Until 1948 the provinces and municipalities also paid virtually the full cost of maintaining traditional services and developing new programs in response to public demand.
Note that new programs came into being not to satisfy the social or political philosophy of any particular group or party, but in response to public demand. Then I wish hon. members to note this important paragraph in the introduction:
An important change in the basis of support for ' new services was made in May, 1948, when the government of Canada announced the introduction of a system of grants to provincial authorities for the extension and improvement of facilities and services as a preliminary step in the development-
Development of what?
-of a national health insurance plan.
Surely this amendment does not go beyond what we find in the government of Canada's health reference book of 1948. I also have before me the health reference book prepared for the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, August, 1945. It is a very instructive document, full of statistics and information on the health of the Canadian people and health services in Canada. The paragraph I wish to read is on page 47

and has the heading, "Summary of Opinions Regarding Health Insurance". It reads as follows:
Recommendations made to the social security committee in 1943 and 1944 are summarized in the accompanying diagram, the most striking feature of which is the almost unanimous support given to the principle of health insurance by organizations presenting briefs and evidence.
This is referring to health insurance organized by whom? A health insurance plan organized by the government of Canada. It continues:
Only one organization was quite opposed to health insurance, and another group requested exemption of its members on religious grounds.
I remember quite well the evidence given before the committee because I was a member of the committee. I wish to say again that the proposal contained in the amendment moved by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) does not go beyond what the government itself has been advocating. Whether or not they believe in it I do not know, but that is what they have been advocating, and I can only assume they do believe in it. Then I come to a perhaps more important document, the proposals of the government of Canada in August, 1945, to the dominion ^provincial conference on reconstruction. At page 28 there is a section dealing with the national health program. This is not a provincial or municipal program; this is the national health program. The subheading is, "Scope for Improvement in Health and Health Services". It reads as follows:
Although great progress has been made in Canada during the first half of this century, there still remains a tremendous job to be done in improving the national health and in extending the benefits of modern science and medical care to all parts of the nation and all sections of the population.
The tremendous job mentioned in this document has hardly been started, let alone completed. What the amendment moved this morning does is to regret that that has not been done. There is not the slightest ground for saying that this amendment proposes that all matters pertaining to health be under the authority of the national government. Let me read again from the same page as follows:
There are great inequalities in the quantity and quality of health care available to different groups of Canadians, and in the costs of such public and private health services and medical and hospital facilities as are now available. These inequalities in part reflect differences in personal incomes, and in part are due to differences between rural and urban areas. Great differences between provinces arise from these same factors.
I noticed that when the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) spoke he said that the government of Alberta was providing a large range of public health services. My congratulations to the province of Alberta not only on
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis providing those services, but on being able to provide them. Then the hon. member went on to say that the government of Alberta was doing that without taxation. Even if Social Credit philosophy was being carried out by the government of Alberta, which it is not, I am firmly convinced that they could not carry out a program of health or any other service without taxation unless they had an alternative source of revenue. Fortunately for the people of Alberta they have an alternative source of revenue at the present time in the form of oil, but every province in Canada has not oil to draw on to provide funds for social services.
My own native province, the province of Prince Edward Island, has no oil wells from which it can finance social services. The province of Manitoba has no great oil wells, nor have the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There are scarcely any of the other provinces which can finance their governmental activities through the sale of oil. I say to the hon. member for Peace River that there is a limited amount of oil under the ground in Alberta. I do not care how much oil there is, the minute the first well was tapped they began to diminish the amount of oil under the ground. Some day they will find out that they have reached the bottom and they will have to turn to some other source of revenue to finance their social and other services.
As the hon. member for Peace River has said, I believe that people should do certain things for themselves. But before people can do things for themselves they must have the ability to do them. Social services are made necessary because people have not that ability. There is perhaps only one reason why a government should engage in any of these services and that is that the people as individuals are not able to provide the services for themselves. The moment there is a large number of people who cannot provide themselves with the things that are generally available within the country, then governments will have to step in because of public need and public demands. They must do this, not necessarily because they wish, but because the needs of the people compel them to do it whether or not it is in their political and social programs.
I believe and have believed for a long time that instead of being curers of disease which they cannot cure, doctors should be teachers of health. However, as long as medical doctors, the same as any other economic group, make their living out of disease I cannot see that they are going to waste a great deal of time in promoting health.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it would be fitting to mention the progress made with respect to health, in the last few years, with the present system. I have here two articles taken from a great Montreal daily, Le Canada, of August 22 last. The first is entitled: Fruitful Federal-Provincial Co-operation
The death rate resulting from tuberculosis has been reduced by half in the province of Quebec from 1941 to 1950. It is quite natural that we should rejoice at such results. Unfortunately, the

present government will immediately want to. claim all the credit. In truth, part of the credit for this improvement is undoubtedly due to the government, but such improvement would not have been possible, during that period, without the vigorous fight undertaken against tuberculosis by the Taschereau government under the leadership of Mr. Athanase David.
The establishment of sanitary units, the popularization of B.C.G. ' and other means of fighting tuberculosis in which Mr. David took the initiative, could not bring immediate results. The governments which succeeded Mr. Taschereau's, those of Messrs. Godbout and Duplessis, carried on his work in favour of health.
We disapprove of many of the actions of the Union Nationale government, of the electoral methods of that party and of the continual boasting of its leader, but we note with pleasure that, in matters of health, Ottawa and Quebec, under any government, get along beautifully for the common good.
Thus, in 1945, with the unanimous approval of the legislative assembly, the government inaugurated a five-year health program. Financial help was not lacking from the central power; on the contrary, under the heading of tuberculosis control alone, it received more than $2 million; for the construction or expansion of hospitals, and of sanatoriums for consumptives, Quebec obtained from Ottawa nearly $8 million.
Last year alone, in the province of Quebec 1,372,800 persons were X-rayed in mobile clinics, dispensaries, county health units and general hospitals. One could hardly ask for better work in tracking down the disease.
Ten years ago, in the province of Quebec, 81 persons out of every 100,000 died from tuberculosis. Last year the proportion was down to 42. That is all we wish to remember, and we rejoice over that fact.	,
I have another item from the same newspaper, Le Canada of Montreal, in which it is remembered that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is a benefactor of humanity. The item was published on August 24 and is entitled:
Benefits of Federal Health Grants
It is interesting to point out the notable development of mental health clinical services now taking place in Canada, mostly for children and adolescents. Nearly forty of these clinics have already been established throughout the country and others are being planned, thanks to the federal government's grants.
Another service which will prove to be of great importance is an instruction course in mental health for experienced teachers in primary and secondary schools. The men and women attending this course will qualify as instructors in mental health for the teaching staff. They will also act as liaison officers between the schools and the mental health clinic in their district. The federal minister of health will pay the teachers giving the special course. He will also award scholarships in order to allow teaching personnel to attend this course.
The mental health grant is but one of the ten grants provided by Ottawa to help provinces extend and improve their public health services. More than $31,000,000 is available each year for this purpose and the provinces are availing themselves more and more of those funds. Federal grants go to the following fields of activity; mental health, cancer control, tuberculosis control, general public

health, venereal diseases, crippled children, research work concerning public health and professional training.
If all the provinces continue to benefit fully from the money placed at their disposal under the national health program, the number and the quality of health services will improve greatly throughout the country. More than 20,000 hospital beds have been added to those already existing; the fight against cancer has been launched for the first time in several provinces and developed in others; medical research and training of medical personnel have been speeded up in the last three years. Public health authorities consider this federal grants program as the most memorable event of its kind on the continent.
Mr. Speaker, I have a third article I wish to read- This is taken from the leading editorial of a great Quebec city daily L'Action Catho-lique, in its November 2 issue. It is signed by the editor in chief of that paper, Dr. Louis-Philippe Roy, who pays a well deserved tribute to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. This followed a conference which had taken place two days previously in Quebec. Here is the article:
To Centralize is to Weaken Confederation
"To weaken the provinces by having recourse to centralization would be to weaken confederation at the same time. As regards the administration of the federal state, or, for that matter of any other state, simplicity and success are inseparable. The duty of any government is to seek the good of the people, not its own power." Then the Hon. Mr. Martin continues immediately;
"It has always been my conviction that Canadians, taken individually, should act as much as possible on their own initiative; that the family and the local community should be free to undertake those things that come under their own jurisdiction, in their own proper sphere; and that the federal government should undertake nothing that the provinces can do better than they can. The one and only purpose of federal health grants is to strengthen and support the provincial health services. Co-operation and not centralization, such is the main idea of the national health program."
The family is the best agency . . .
. . . says Dr. Roy.
This policy implies another: We must let the family do what it can do. "No welfare agency", said the Hon. Mr. Martin, "can take the place of the parents. The family is the best agency to which the care of any child should be entrusted. However, if such care is to be satisfactory, the family must have an income commensurate with its obligations".
This does not mean the Minister of National Health and Welfare underestimates the tremendous services rendered by many welfare organizations, "but", he adds, "when the fundamental needs of children are at stake, I believe that the family is best equipped to look after them, provided it has the required economic resources."
The express purpose of family allowances is to provide parents with a part of the resources they lack. Experience shows that the government was right in entrusting the allowances directly to parents, abuses being comparatively rare.
Mr. Martin's whole conference was characterized by broad-mindedness and a Christian and social spirit. It is fitting that this be noted and that the minister be congratulated. Let us hope that the excellent principles he mentioned will be applied by all his colleagues in the federal government.

It is a remarkable article. It is a fine tribute, one that was well deserved by the minister.

I simply rise for the purpose of explaining why I propose to vote against the amendment. I do so in the hope that, with the oversimplification that sometimes occurs, I will not see the statement made that in doing so we have voted against any national health plan. That is not before us. We have indicated our position very clearly in regard to adequate plans for maintaining and preserving the health of our people and offering to the people of Canada the very highest level of hospital and other facilities. I think that the position of our party was very clearly and very briefly stated on March 4, 1949, when, in discussing this very subject, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) had this to say. I am quoting from page 1154 of Hansard of Friday, March 4, 1949:
This party has long realized the necessity for a plan of health in the Dominion of Canada. Let there be no doubt where this party stands on that now. We stand in favour of a plan which, in co-operation with the provinces, will give the people the maximum of services, and yet be a plan of freedom, where the doctors will not be civil servants, and which will allow free choice between doctor and patient. We have got a full realization of the deficiencies in treatment services in Canada and in our preventive services, and we stand ready to implement a plan to overcome these deficiencies, and which will raise health standards in Canada to the equal of that in any other country of the world.
Without amplifying that statement, or seeking to go into further detail, I simply wish to say that this does represent a compact statement of the position of our party in regard to measures of this nature. We want to see provisions by which the health of our people will be advanced in every way that it is within the power of the government to assist. We want to see the opportunity afforded to every Canadian to have appropriate hospital service and to have the very highest level of medical treatment, no matter what their conditions in life may be. However, I would point out the statement on that occasion contained words which should not be forgotten in a discussion of this subject, namely, "in co-operation with the provinces." We must not forget that under our federal constitution 94699-116J
The Address-Mr. Drew health and civil hospitalization are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial governments. It is not competent for the dominion government, or for the parliament of Canada, to deal with over-all plans of this kind, or to introduce measures which would put into effect even the most admirable program, unless that had been done in consultation with and in agreement with the provincial governments, and ultimately the legislatures of the provinces.
The amendment now before us amounts to a vote of want of confidence on the ground that the government has failed to make provision for a national health plan. That does not mean that it has taken the proper steps to advance a measure of this nature; it suggests that steps should have been taken in the present speech from the throne to provide a national health plan. No matter what any one of us in this house may think of the government's failure to advance further than it has in consultation with the provinces, the fact is that this subject has not reached a point where it would be possible to present a plan to this house because the provinces have not yet had an opportunity formally to approve of any plan. Nothing would be more unlikely to prevent the implementation of an effective plan than to proceed in a manner which might be regarded by the provinces as an arbitrary attempt to place on record an established plan and then simply ask for their approval or rejection.
Having said that, I wish to indicate my own belief that this is a subject which should be explored as expeditiously as possible. It is necessary to carry on extensive surveys and inquiries to find out what the best methods are that could be employed in this country of ours. One aspect of this problem alone which has not been adequately explored in relation to any plans of this kind is the disparity between the financial strength of one provincial legislature and another. As has already been pointed out, some provinces have available to them great natural resources from which they derive revenue to an extent that makes it possible for them to undertake programs which other provinces might not be able to undertake, no matter how much they might desire to follow precisely the same course. Any plan introduced which can properly be described as a national plan must be one which recognizes that difference, and which assures throughout the whole of Canada an equal measure of opportunity, or as nearly an equal measure as is practicable, so that every Canadian may have his or her health protected and preserved.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take not more than five minutes of the time of the house to bring to the government's attention something which I believe is a matter of very great national importance. I refer to the alarming state of unpreparedness in our civil defence program.
I feel sure all hon. members were deeply impressed when they read about the program which the city of New York has worked out, and which was put to the actual test a short time ago. The people of New York have faced a very real threat in a very practical way. And what the people of New York have done, we here in Canada can also do if we are given real leadership by the government.
While visiting the city of Edmonton this summer, I learned of the great apprehension felt by the people of that city regarding the possibility of air attack. They feel particularly vulnerable to air attacks from Russia, because during the last war on many occasions they actually saw Russian pilots walking their streets. They know how easy it is to fly from Russia to Edmonton, and back again. They are greatly worried indeed because nothing of a practical nature has been done to protect their great oil centre and air terminal from the possibility of air attack.
The people of Toronto and Montreal are similarly apprehensive. They are worried because nothing of a practical nature has been done to protect those vital centres of production. I feel sure that people in similarly vulnerable centres share the same apprehension. I feel it is essential that every effort be made to maintain our productive capacity. We are obliged to do this if we are to carry out the commitments to NATO we have

undertaken, because that whole program is so dependent upon the productive capacity of this country.
It is not enough for the federal government merely to contribute to the cost of civil defence. The federal government must give leadership in the building up of our civil defences. It is true that the co-operation of the provinces and municipalities is not only necessary but essential. However, the primary responsibility for the defence of the civilian population of this country rests squarely upon the shoulders of the federal government.
To the extent that our government assures a satisfactory civil defence program can we be assured of an uninterrupted continuation of our productive capacity, upon which our preparedness program depends. I call upon the government to give this country a civil defence program of which we can be truly proud-instead of feeling ashamed, as I for one, and many other people, feel today.
What this country wants is leadership and a practical plan. What we are getting are bland assurances that everything is all right, coupled with a shocking state of unpreparedness.

I should like to put on the record the short form of the address to His Excellency in order that the record might be quite clear. Omitting the preamble, the short form reads as follows:
May it please Your Excellency:
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled, beg leave to offer our humble thanks to Your Excellency for the gracious speech which Your Excellency has addressed to both houses of parliament.
That form of address has been in use in this country since 1903 without any change. In fact there has been no addition to the address presented to His Excellency in the 85 years of the existence of this country except in 1899, to which incident I shall refer in a minute or two. The practice in Great Britain has been to move a short address similar to the one which I have quoted, and this practice has been followed ever since 1891, except on occasions when the government of the day resigned.
To those who may say that there is no particular importance to be attached to that, I reply that this strikes at the root of our parliamentary rules and procedure. If we are to consider that this particular established custom is of no concern then we will be led to say that other established customs similarly are of no concern and the book of rules and established parliamentary procedure may be considerably disturbed. I have no objection to changes in the rules and parliamentary procedure when they are founded upon reason and are fully debated, but this procedure is being rushed through at this time without full consideration.
As I understand it, parliamentary rules and procedure exist for the protection of the rights of minorities. One can look forward to the rights of future minorities being in danger. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, if the practice now to be incorporated into our procedure is

I think there should be some revision of our method of procedure with respect to the sipeech from the throne. This is necessary in view of the criticism inside and out of the house of the length of time taken in debates here. I would refer those who are interested to Beauchesne's third edition, page 96, paragraph 226, where the subject of the address in reply to the speech from the throne is considered. On that page will be found a short quotation from a speech made by the Hon. Mr. McKenzie, as follows:
It has been thought desirable in our parliamentary practice that it is better to postpone debates upon specific subjects of discussion in the house until those matters are brought forward before us by a bill or resolution.
Speaking on the address in 1879 Sir John Macdonald said:
1 am glad the opposition have adopted the English modem system-a very proper one-of passing the address without amendment, and when all the various subjects alluded to in it are dealt with, when the measures proposed are before the house, they and their details can be criticized with a full knowledge and satisfactory explanation with regard to the policy of the government.
I suggest that there is a field for investigation with regard to the procedure followed in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne.
I should like to say a word, Mr. Speaker, about the precedent of 1899 which has brought us to this impasse. Unfortunately no one in the House of Commons objected to the form of that amendment during the debate. It was a lengthy debate, covering twenty days. The subject was controversial and followed the discovery of gold in the Yukon and consequent charges of maladministration there. No one objected to the type of amendment that

was presented on that occasion, and consequently we are confronted with a situation where we feel that a somewhat similar plan could be adopted here. I point out, as was pointed out by the member from Lake Centre, that a different method of dealing with the address was followed in those days. The address in reply to the speech from the throne followed almost word for word the speech from the throne itself. It was divided into paragraphs which were numbered, and there was a debate on each paragraph.
The amendment of 1899 was attached as paragraph No. 10. There had been nine paragraphs written into the resolution, and this was attached as paragraph No. 10. To cite another example, in 1902 Mr. Bourassa moved an amendment to paragraph No. 5, but subsequently withdrew that amendment so it did not establish any precedent. However, that was the method of conducting the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the thrqne in those days, that is up until 1902. Since 1903 we have had this short form of address, and there has been no means of moving amendments to particular items in the speech from the throne. Consequently, general amendments expressing want of confidence have been moved. Those, of course, have been considerable in number.
Now, how can the house extricate itself from this position? The only example that I have been able to find or that has been drawn to my attention is a procedure that was followed in England in 1894, to which reference has been made in this house. This is what happened on that occasion. There was a Liberal government in the house with the Conservatives as the official opposition, Liberal unionists, Irish nationalists and some independents. It was a rather mixed group, and the amendment on that occasion was moved by Mr. Labouchere. I am not sure of his position in the house, but I believe he was an independent. The government supporters in the house favoured the subject matter of the amendment, so it was passed and attached to the short address. In 1894 the short address read as follows:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in parliament assembled, beg leave to thank Your Majesty for the most gracious speech which Your Majesty has addressed to both houses of parliament.
To that short address was attached an amendment concerning the restriction of the power of the House of Lords. The government felt that it could not present that amendment to His Majesty, and could find no precedent for an address that had been

amended without the resignation of the government. The government was not resigning, so at the particular stage which we have now reached, the government of the day, assisted by His Majesty's loyal opposition, voted down the main motion as amended and Sir William Harcourt immediately introduced the following short form of address:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the commons of the United Kingdom and Ireland in parliament assembled, humbly assure Your Majesty that the measures recommended to our consideration shall receive our most careful attention and we beg leave to thank Your Majesty for the most gracious speech which Your Majesty has addressed to both houses of parliament.
That short form of resolution was then passed. I suggest that on this occasion, perhaps through an error in procedure-I am not referring to the Speaker's ruling but an error in procedure in the house-we have reached the stage where the address has been amended. Surely, the only way to extricate ourselves is to do the same thing as was done in England in 1894. The house should vote down the main motion as amended, and the government should introduce a new address in short form with just a minor alteration. This could be passed, and then we would be in keeping with the established tradition of the House of Commons.
Alternatively, if that course does not meet with favour, we should have a statement recorded on Hansard that this is not to be considered as a precedent, so that future parliaments will not look to this occasion as a guide. In this way, sir, I submit that no stifling precedent will be established which will interfere with the privileges and rights of the house. We shall maintain the long-established form of presenting an address to His Excellency, and the prestige of the House of Commons, which is at stake, will be maintained in high favour. We must recognize the fact that the House of Commons comes in for criticism from people on the outside, and we may be made to look ridiculous on this occasion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
I beg to submit the motions
required by standing order 57 for the setting up of the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means. I move:
That this house will at its next sitting resolve itself into a committee to consider of a supply to be granted to His Majesty.
I also move:
That this house will at its next sitting resolve itself into a committee to consider of the ways and means for raising the supply to be granted to His Majesty.
May we have some explanation as to why these motions are necessary?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because standing order
57 requires them.

Mr. Speaker, the rules require a number of procedures in an orderly and sensibly conducted session, but in. this particular session, where there has been no budget and nothing calling for these motions, I think members should be told why they are necessary, no matter what may be contemplated in the case of a regular session.

I might remind the house
that these motions are not debatable. There are two motions. One is to set up the committee to consider the supply to be granted to His Majesty and the other is respecting ways and means. Will the house receive both motions at the same time?
Agreed.

I am not debating these
motions, but I should like to have some indication as to what supply is being called for.
Read the rules.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Standing order 57 reads:
The house shall appoint the committees of supply and ways and means, at the commencement of every session, so soon as an address has been agreed to, in- answer to His Excellency's speech.
"At the commencement of every session" means just as soon as the various motions, amendments, subamendments and votes can be disposed of, and this time there have been a great many. Under the standing order these motions could not be moved until the address had been adopted, and the rule requires that it be done as soon, as the address is adopted. I am submitting them at the time required by the standing order. The house knows that it is not the intention of the government to submit a budget at this session, and there may be no occasion for anything to be dealt with by the committees; nevertheless they are required to be set up by the rule.	.

I simply repeat that I am not
debating the question-
Oh, oh.

-but while the rules may call for a certain procedure, that procedure must have some relation to reality. The rule that has been read relates to the procedure having to do with the introduction of a budget. I submit if there is to be no budget these motions have no meaning.

house to adopt the motions?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Can the minister tell us whether the board of transport commissioners has jurisdiction over any other tolls on canals, or tolls of a similar nature?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Yes. I speak of course from memory, but I believe that some time ago the Transport Act was amended in order to give the board of transport commissioners jurisdiction over tolls on the Mackenzie river.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Then the only ship tolls over which it has any jurisdiction at the present time are the tolls on the Mackenzie river?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: They also have certain jurisdiction under part II of the Transport Act.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I ask that because this would seem to be breaking new ground for the board. They will have to consider a new type of rate in connection, with these tolls. I wonder whether this is the beginning of a policy of turning the control of shipping over to the board of transport commissioners?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I do not think this is breaking new ground in so far as the board of transport commissioners is concerned. My colleague draws my attention to the fact that the board does not fix these tolls. The authority will fix them and file them, but they are subject to the jurisdiction of the board under section 52.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: These tolls are to be adjudicated upon in much the same way as freight rates, are they not?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: If anyone complains that the tolls are unfair, that complaint is presented to the board of transport commissioners which could rule against the tolls, in which event the St. Lawrence authority would have to change them. Will that be the position?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Not quite. After deciding whether or not rates as fixed by the authority are unjustly discriminatory, the board of transport commissioners would then report to the authority.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: If the finding of the board is to be merely a recommendation and not an order, are we not putting the board of transport commissioners in a position which is not very sound?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
I think not. The tolls have to be fixed with reference to the capitalization of this scheme. If the board of transport commissioners perchance were to recommend 94699-1171
St. Lawrence Waterway that tolls be lowered to an extent that would make it impossible to amortize the scheme, pay the interest and operating charges, then the authority might well not accept that recommendation. There is still the provision of section 52 for appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I want to ask a question with reference to what was said the other day in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra about cabotage. I understood the minister to say that United States ships would not be allowed to pick up trade in a Canadian port for delivery to another Canadian port. My attention has been drawn to the fact that ships operated by the Chicago Tribune, which is owned by Colonel McCormick, are carrying pulpwood or pulp products from the lower St. Lawrence port of Baie Comeau to Thorold in Ontario.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I should like to look into that because it would be contrary to the rules of cabotage.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Would it be possible under this clause to have a differential in the tolls charged a ship plying between two Canadian ports under Canadian registry and a ship under foreign registry?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I bring that up because that was one of the extremely contentious issues when the Panama canal was constructed. The United States, which built the canal, for many years had a differential in favour of United States ships because it was contended that ships moving between the east and west coasts were intercoastal ships and therefore should not have to pay tolls. I was wondering if a ship plying from a lower St. Lawrence port to a port on the upper lakes would pay exactly the same toll as a ship of foreign registry coming in from some other continent and carrying goods to an upper lakes port.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
