maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
That is sufficient for my submission. There does not seem to be a provision anywhere for a report to parliament; parliament is left entirely out of the picture. Secondly, there is no provision in the bill for calling for tenders for work to be done. Both these provisions are contained in the National Harbours Board Act, chapter 42 of the statutes of 1936. As the minister knows, section 32 of that act reads:
The board shall, as soon as possible but within three months after the termination of each calendar year, submit an annual report to the minister in such form as he may prescribe and the minister shall lay the said report before parliament.
Section 12 of the same act provides for the calling of tenders, and I should like to quote subsection 1 which reads:
(1) Whenever any works are to be executed under the direction of the board, the board shall call tenders by public advertisement for the execution of such works, except in cases
(a)	of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest: or
(b)	in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously or economically executed by the officers and servants of the board or of His Majesty; or
(c)	where the estimated cost of the work is less than ten thousand dollars.
That is the provision for the calling of tenders in the case of the national harbours board. I suggest to the minister that some similar provisions should be written into *this bill covering, first of all, a report to parliament and, secondly, the calling of tenders. Here we have an authority being set up which will spend an amount of money perhaps equal to the amount spent on all the national harbours of Canada. I have not had time to check the amount of money expended on the national harbours, but I would doubt that it is as large as the amount involved in the St. Lawrence seaway. I think it is a

very sound principle that this authority, which is to have such vast powers and is to control such a big project, should report annually to parliament. We must not get these bodies away from the control of parliament.
In this bill there is not even provision for a report to the minister. In the case of the national harbours board, I know it is helpful to get that report each year. I submit that parliament certainly is entitled to get a report from this authority in some way, and I hope the government will agree to an amending section providing for such report.
I would point out to the minister also that this bill contains no provision for the publication of regulations passed by this authority. The national harbours board has to do that, and I see no reason why there should not be some provision in this seaway bill for the publication in the Canada Gazette of the regulations which are passed by the authority.
With regard to the provision making it necessary to call for tenders, we have been getting farther and farther away from that good old-fashioned practice. Time and time again exceptions are made. Here is an authority which is to spend a great deal of our money, and I feel there should be a provision set out in the bill forcing the authority to call for tenders with, of course, whatever exceptions are reasonable. Such a provision seems to have been completely overlooked in this bill, and I believe that is a great mistake. If there is to be no such provision then it will be hard to justify insisting upon calling for tenders for many other types of work, and in my opinion this is a departure from a good practice.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: On the last point raised by the hon. member, namely the reference to a report to parliament, if he looks at section 25 which has to do with the guarantee of loans he will see that when a loan or guarantee is made under that section, parliament must authorize it. There will be, therefore, an opportunity for discussion. Again with reference to the point he raised, the hon. member is not without knowledge that the financial administration measure, which is in the committee on public accounts, provides for an annual report being made to parliament by all crown companies. It is not necessary, therefore, to put a provision in this bill. The object of the financial administration bill is to consolidate the financial aspects of all crown companies so they would have to make annual reports to parliament, and so there could be a greater check on their finances by the department concerned. I believe that meets the point.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: That might be good enough in the case of the ordinary crown company, but here we have one set up by statute, and it is probably the most important crown company under dominion authority. What this financial bill will contain by the time it passes the house is open to question. It is still in the public accounts committee, and may very well not pass the house at this session. I believe a provision should be written into this bill that a report will be presented annually to parliament. There are not very many of these companies which do report annually.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Every one of them reports annually.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: To parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: The national harbours board reports, I know, because I am interested in the Vancouver harbour. There is a report every year, and I find it helpful. I see no reason why there should not be a similar provision in this bill.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: There is no intention that this company will not report to parliament, and I hope the hon. member will not think there is. The point I am making is that there is provision already for all crown companies to report to parliament, under the financial administration bill. For that reason I do not think it is necessary to have a duplication. However, I am not saying that I am going to oppose it. I think it is redundant.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: It is not a redundancy yet, because the other bill has not been passed, and it might not be passed at this session.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

The reason a section concerning tenders was not put in the bill is that it may be necessary to do a great deal of the work with our own equipment. maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think the minister should object to introducing this
St. Lawrence Waterway amended section. In the first place, this is not a crown corporation in the ordinary sense of that term. Crown corporations are corporations of the type which usually contemplate the development of a particular enterprise with limited scope, important though it may be. This is a great national venture, and is comparable in many ways with the development and operation of publicly-owned power and other projects of that kind. Certainly there should be a provision for the calling of tenders. There could be the same reservation as there is in the National Harbours Board Act, and as is contained in other acts concerning the use of government equipment under the Department of Public Works where that becomes desirable. I do not believe we should be called upon to rely on a general provision calling for an annual statement, because this is an extremely important operation. maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 34, respecting construction of works for the generation of electrical power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: I was just going to say that this is the bill concerning the development of power in the international rapids section of the river. I do not propose to make a lengthy statement for the reason that both resolutions were considered together, and to a large extent I think both bills are being considered together. All this does is implement an agreement made between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Ontario. There are only four clauses in it, the first having to do with the approval by this parliament of the agreement; the next giving power to the province of Ontario to transfer certain lands, and likewise to Canada; the third gives certain powers to the hydro-electric power commission, and gives to the Power Commission Act of Ontario the same powers of expropriation mutatis mutandis as have been contained in the Expropriation Act of Canada. In other words, what this does is confirm the agreement entered into between the two governments of Ontario and Canada for the development of power in the international rapids section of the river.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is completely complementary to the other, and it would be unthinkable if one were considered without the other. As a matter of fact they are and must be considered as a joint plan. What I shall have to say on this subject at this time will be short,


but I feel that the record should contain some statistics of the growth of the load of power and the demand for power in Ontario. I shall endeavour very briefly to put that on the record to show how desperately this power is needed in Ontario at the present time.
I think some hon. members do not realize what has happened in Canada since the end of the war. The figures for population, the figures for growth of industry, and the figures for growth of load for primary power I think are probably outstanding for any country in the world. In 1940 the load in Ontario was 2,116,600 horsepower; in 1945, that is at the end of the war,, it had grown to 2,597,400 horsepower; but in 1950, that is in half a decade since the war, it had grown to 3,659,900 horsepower. In other words, in the period since the war the primary load in Ontario has grown no less than 41 per cent. In that period of five years the extra power load very nearly equalled half the total load in Ontario at the end of the war. While figures for gross provincial production show in dollar value an even more astounding gross, there is some degree of reduction owing to the inflated dollar and the lower purchasing power of the dollar. In 1945, however, the gross provincial production was $3-97 billion, while in 1950 this had grown to an estimated $6 * 55 billion, or an increase over 1945 of 64 per cent.
I mention this to show the growth of industrial output which runs concurrently with the growth of primary power, and how these two essential factors in our development run hand in hand. One is complementary to the other, and I give this as an example of why it is necessary and desirable for us to develop all possible sources of primary power, wherever they may be located in Canada. To give an example of this growth, and to show the current rate of increase in growth, let me point out that the gross primary load per 20-minute peak, on a date at the beginning of this session, was 415,086 horsepower greater than the same day a year ago. Or, to express it in another way, it was 32,400 horsepower greater than the Toronto average load for the month, including Leaside. In other words every year the total load for Ontario is growing at a rate equal to the total load for greater Toronto. We think that is an astounding development. It would appear that the load in this province is growing at a rate equal to the load of what is certainly the second, and perhaps is now the leading, industrial city in Canada. That is an example of the astounding growth of the load in Ontario.

Since the end of the war in 1945 there have been installed 1,112,700 horsepower of primary hydroelectric power. There are under contract and under construction
970,000	horsepower. I am using the horsepower unit rather than that of the kilowatt, because the former is a somewhat easier lay term. The same plants, now either completed or under construction, will add a further 892,000 horsepower, or a total under construction of 1,862,000 horsepower. This makes a grand total of 2,975,000 horsepower added or under construction at the present time in Ontario. When one considers the enormous construction that has been undertaken by the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission, if he did not appreciate the tremendous growth in this area he would conclude that there would be comparative security for at least the medium distant future. But at the present rate of growth, assuming we do not get an acceleration over the 1950 rate of growth-and that is not being borne out-there will be a further power shortage in Ontario in 1957. As we are now in the year 1951, we have at the very outside five years of grace before there may be a further power shortage in Ontario, despite the fact that there has been added or is being added nearly 3 million additional horsepower since the end of the war.
I believe that growth will compare favourably with the growth of any other area at any period, anywhere in the world. I very much doubt if comparable figures anywhere else have ever been established.
Now let us come to the next question, what it will mean if we are denied that power. The cost of steam power is approximately three times the cost of power developed on the St. Lawrence river. Using construction costs of 1949, we may assume that hydroelectric power can be produced on the bus bars at the plant for approximately 3 mills per kilowatt hour. Taking steam at the then rate, we find that the cost will be slightly over 7J mills per kilowatt hour. The original figure for hydroelectric power was 2 mills per kilowatt hour, but to be on the safe side it has been estimated that construction costs will now make it 3 mills per kilowatt hour.
Besides the extra cost to the consumer, there is the problem with steam power of obtaining coal. Certainly the coal for the Windsor generating plant, and up to now, I believe, for the Toronto generating plant, has been purchased from the United States, which further puts out of balance our balance of payments position with that country. Therefore both from the point of view of
St. Lawrence Power Development cheap power and the balance of payments position with the United States it is imperative that this work be proceeded with as soon as possible. I do not propose to go into the figures in detail with respect to the use of power in Ontario and the use of power by the Hydro Electric Power Commission. However, the figures show that nowhere in the world is there such high consumption of electrical energy on a per capita basis as there is in Ontario. This has been brought about progressively and aggressively by the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission, who deserve the greatest credit for the work they have done not only for the industrial and urban consumer but particularly for the farm consumer. I think the record of farm electrification in Ontario is unique anywhere in the world-. They have done this as a public trust in such a way as to make Ontario hydro the best servant the people of Ontario could possibly have.
I mention these facts merely to put them on the record at this juncture. They have all been given before by the chairman of the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission,. Mr. Saunders, and by others; but I also do so to show hon. members in the house who do not come from Ontario the growth of the load and the tremendous increase in productivity which has been brought about by cheap and abundant hydroelectric energy. I also do so to show hon. members who do not come from Ontario that it should be a primary function of every provincial government to endeavour to develop every waterpower resource it has, because with the addition of abundant and cheap electrical energy there is phenomenally increased production and population. In other words, it is largely upon electrical energy that the amazing prosperity of Canada has been built, and I hope this project, like the other, will be proceeded with as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing this resolution to amend the National Gallery of Canada Act, may I recall that the national gallery, along with the Royal Canadian Academy of Arts, was established in 1880. For the first twenty-six years of its existence the national gallery made little progress; it had no permanent home, few pictures of any significance, no purchase grant and no qualified staff.
In 1907 the government of the day decided that art had an important place to play in Canadian life and in that year, by order in council, the government established the advisory arts council, composed of three leading citizens prominent in the art field of this country. The council was charged with the duty of advising the minister on all purchases for the national gallery, and on the construction of public monuments and the acquisition of other works of art for the government. The council fulfilled its duty well. A qualified curator was employed and the national gallery grew rapidly and soundly by the able handling of the modest grants made by parliament for purchases from year to year.
In 1913 the national gallery was incorporated by act of parliament. The advisory arts council became a board of trustees to manage and develop the national gallery under the supervision of the Minister of Public Works. The act of 1913 proved to be a very satisfactory piece of legislation and served its purpose acceptably for many years, during which time regional art galleries fostered by the national gallery were established in many parts of the country. During that time also the work of Canadian artists became wideband favourably known in most countries of the world, and Canadian public interest in the fine arts showed a most encouraging growth, as described in the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, popularly
referred to as the Massey report.
*
During these thirty-eight years the national gallery, from a practically unknown institution, has come to be widely recognized, not only at home but also abroad, by reason of its unique extension service, which I believe is superior to that of any similar institution in the world. Its collections have been reviewed from time to time by some

National Gallery
of the world's best experts and it is agreed, I am informed, that they are among the finest of the smaller collections on this continent. These pictures are widely lent throughout the country under appropriate conditions, and it is expected that this extension work of the gallery will increase from year to year, as foreshadowed in the Massey report.
It is to implement some of the leading recommendations of that report that the present bill is being introduced. The new act preserves the substance of the act of 1913, with a number of important improvements. The board, which for many years was composed of three trustees, was in 1922 increased to five members, but may now, under the present bill, consist of from five to nine members, reflecting the country's wider interest in the institution.
A new section provides that the national gallery purchase grant will not lapse at the end of the fiscal year, but that purchase funds may be accumulated from year to year for important additions to the national collection. This provision will facilitate the work of the board, and put the national gallery more nearly on an equality with competing galleries. Section 4 (1) provides that appointments to the national gallery staff shall be made by the civil service commission, which has been the practice followed by the board for the past thirty years. Clause 3 (4) gives the board the power, with the approval of the minister, to sell, lease, exchange or otherwise dispose of any property which it is not considered desirable to retain in the national gallery.
The bill also makes provision for the design in industry section established on an experimental basis four years ago. This branch was formed to study the problems of industrial design with the objective of raising the design quality of Canadian manufactured products.
To sum up, this bill gives the national gallery greater opportunity to foster and encourage public interest in the fine and applied arts. I am sure the house would like this institution to be able to play an increasingly important role in our national life.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask one or two questions and make one or two observations. Perhaps the minister will tell us a little more concerning what is meant by "entering into contracts", or perhaps that has no significance beyond what he has said already.
At a time when we are asked to concentrate so much on, and to make such ample material

provisions for matters of defence, matters of social security and all the other matters which come before us and which are so pressing, it is perhaps difficult to convince ourselves that a matter of this kind, which cannot be assessed in any material terms, can be equally pressing. Yet I think a moment's reflection will enable us to realize that it is important. I suppose one of the things of which we are most constantly reminded is that, in this struggle in which we are engaged, it is not wholly a matter of material things; it is a matter of maintaining the whole fabric and quality of our civilization.
Even those of us who are less competent to express an expert opinion on the importance of art realize that our civilization is made up of things of that kind, things of the spirit. We do realize, too, that our whole civilization would be infinitely poorer if we did not have among us people who are devoting their lives to artistic pursuits, who know about them and who, so to speak, keep the flag flying in respect of those matters. Therefore I am quite sure we shall all welcome what the minister is saying to us, and we shall be anxious that proper steps be taken.
As the minister has already said, the Massey report has brought this and other kindred matters to our minds. However much we may be obsessed with the difficulties of finding money for the other things we are doing, I feel that we must not neglect these things. The more one looks about the more one realizes the many things that are pressing in on our civilization, and the more that some of the sanctions that supported our civilization decades ago are not so strong as they were. It seems to me, too, that we must realize that things such as those for which the national gallery stands must be supported in spite of all the other claims on. our time and our purse. Those are all the remarks I desire to make, Mr. Chairman, but before I sit down I should like to ask the minister if he would answer my question as to whether the word "contracts" has any other significance.

subtopic: INCREASE IN MEMBERSHIP OF BOARD OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while art may be said to be international in its scope, and a great work of art may be said to belong to history, nevertheless increasingly there are individual artists who belong to Canada and who are finding in the Canadian scene much scope for their particular genius. There have come into being also, over the years, associations of creative artists and those who are interested in art. Thus it is a pleasure to note that in Canada we are making progress in a desired direction. It is not so long ago that one heard much talk of the inferiority

complex which bedevilled Canadians in the matter of the arts. In our writing and in our painting we were held, and with some justice, to be mere imitators, mostly of the European or of the British school. If that were once true, I think it is fair to say that it is true no longer; for in our literature and even more in our painting we are becoming more mature, and we are beginning to use art as an expression of Canadianism.
Sir, I know little about art; I am certainly no authority upon it. However, I know what pleases me; and I think that to please must be the first function of art anywhere. In so far as art brings pleasure to the Canadian public or opens up to the masses of our population new vistas of enjoyment-enjoyment which up to the present has been unknown to many of them-I think that art as such should be encouraged.
By reason of its introduction of this bill, it would appear that the Canadian government holds the same view. The very existence of this bill is an acknowledgment on the part of the government that art has become an important phase of our national life. I suppose one might synopsize the provisions of this bill by saying simply they strengthen the hand of the board of trustees of the national gallery of Canada. The bill provides for an increase in the number of members of the board to which I have referred. It provides for added staff which I think is necessary, and it gives the board authority for the making of expenditures which it deems necessary; to that end, funds will be placed at the board's disposal.
It is not my intention to discuss here this evening all the - functions which the board is performing or the functions which it may perform with its facilities increased as they will be by the passage of this bill. But there is one principle I would lay down. Just as a taste for good literature is developed only by the reading of it, so does appreciation of art increase by the viewing of it; it can increase only in that way. If one grants that principle-and there will be few who will deny it-then the opportunity to view good pictures must be brought to the greatest possible number of people. That, increasingly, must be the chief task and the primary responsibility of this board. That undertaking involves a decentralization of activity. There must, of course, be some central source of that activity, namely a central national gallery. Ottawa, the capital of this country, seems to be the logical place for it. That is
National Gallery
where it now is, although the present facilities are much too meagre, and the space is much too limited in what we now call the national gallery.
Such a central point is the natural home for our national collection of paintings; but there must be co-operation between the national gallery and local galleries throughout the country if the principle I have expounded is to be acted upon. From this central gallery there must go out collections which we may be fortunate enough to borrow from other countries abroad, and exhibitions of particular Canadian artists. I commend the board for having already made available to the public of Canada reproductions of great paintings at reasonable prices. I am thinking of the silkscreen prints-I think that is the technical name of them-for public buildings, schools, and other educational institutions throughout the country. These become a source of education in art appreciation, which in turn might become a stimulus and inspiration to artistic endeavour.
Governments are fond of telling us that in all things they must be practical. I am happy that this government and this intensely practical house should give at least transient attention to what are commonly called things cultural.
In this connection may I pay tribute to the Massey commission for its stupendous accomplishment towards encouragement of the arts. The report of that commission has met with a fine response throughout this whole country, and has aroused wide interest among the Canadian people. I have not yet had time to read what it recommends in the matter of a national gallery, but from a study of other parts of the report in which I was greatly interested, I can anticipate with confidence the soundness of those recommendations.
We are pleased to support this bill as a group, and are pleased to endorse the request of the board and other interested organizations for a new and satisfying national gallery. We in this C.C.F. group, and particularly our leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, have on many occasions espoused the cause of the arts. We have not only advocated for Ottawa a great national gallery worthy of this nation, of which we now have only a mere imitation; we have been even more urgent and persistent in our request for a national library of which we have not yet a semblance.
Sir, I think it can be said that we in this country have reached the end of the pioneer stage. Canada has grown up. Canada is a

National Gallery
great and wealthy nation. The needs of the body-if I may think of the matter in human terms-have become satisfied. Let us now reach out for the things of the mind and spirit. May I once more-I have done it before-cite the quotation from St. Augustine which adorns one of the front pages of the fine report to which I have referred:
A nation is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish; therefore, to determine the quality of a nation, you must consider what those things are.
May it be said of this nation in days to come, when history will have had an opportunity to estimate her quality, that she chose early to cherish the right things, the things which make a nation truly great.
We support the resolution with the greatest of pleasure.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, what I have to say will take only a few minutes. The first thing I want to say is that I hope the minister will do everything possible-and this bill gives me the opportunity to say it-to relieve the congestion in the national museum where the art gallery is housed. I agree with him that the art gallery does contain a small but worth-while collection. A great part of it, though, is stored in cases underground. There are some very valuable objects in the museum which never are seen by the public, which are stored in the cellars and in many other places, I understand, in Ottawa. The overcrowding of that building is simply scandalous, and I hope that immediate steps will be taken to do two things. The first thing-I speak here as a mining engineer- is to do something about the proper housing of the geological survey, which is taking a tremendous amount of space in that building. It is not a proper place for the geological survey. They are taking up space that should be given to the scientific work of the museum. I say this because I had several people working in the museum complain to me last year about it.
We want to see the collections we have. Let us not bury them. That is the first thing. The second thing is this. We regard ourselves in Canada, and take much pleasure in considering ourselves, as Philistines. We say we have not much art. We rather think of ourselves as rough-hewn pioneers and that sort of thing. It may interest the committee to know that the famous collection from the Kunsthistorische (art history) museum in Vienna, known on tour as the Hapsburg treasures, showed a profit only in the city of Toronto. The only city on the entire continent of North America where sufficient people showed interest to make the exhibit
[Mr. Knight.1
a profitable and paying venture was Toronto. The other cities across this country, including the main cities in the United States, did not show the same interest as was shown in Toronto. That is something which shows the general interest in art amongst the people of Canada, and belies the happy Philistine idea which we endeavour to cherish amongst ourselves so much.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING TENURE OF OFFICE AND SALARIES OF COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
It is good to know that this function has been added to the many duties of the Minister of Public Works. As the minister knows, in the light of such information as the house was able to get at an earlier stage, some of us on this side found ourselves opposed to the measure forecast by this resolution.
As we understand the measure, it is proposed to take out of the statute setting up the civil service commission any reference to the amount of salary to be paid to the civil service commissioners. Rather, it is planned that their salaries from here on will be fixed by order in council. We are opposed to that move, and we signified our opposition by voting against the motion that Mr. Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on this resolution.
I wish to repeat that I was quite disappointed at the proposal as outlined to us by the Secretary of State. It was a surprise to us. We understood, from the wording of the resolution now before us, that it was a very simple proposal relating to the tenure of office and the salaries of the commissioners. I, for one, thought all that would be proposed would be that the Auditor General's recommendation would be carried out, and that the entire salary of each commissioner would be spelled out in the statute rather than having part of it in the statute and part of it in the annual estimates. However, when we had a brief statement from the Secretary of State it turned out that such was not the intention. Rather it is proposed to take this fixing of the salaries of civil service commissioners away from parliament altogether.
I think it is quite clear that the civil service commissioners should stand in the same relationship to parliament as does the Auditor General and also the chief electoral officer. In respect of each of these other officials it is clearly recognized that they are responsible to parliament, not to the government. They are appointed under that interesting piece of machinery known as the great seal; and they are officers of the whole of parliament rather than officials of the government. The civil service commissioners are not appointed in the same way; but the whole theory of the civil service commission is that government positions should be removed as far as possible from political control. That is a battle that was fought and won many years ago. I think it is an integral part of that situation that the salaries of the civil service commissioners should be fixed not by the government, not by order in council but by parliament.
As I have already indicated, I feel that their relationship to us should be the same as that
Civil Service Act
of the other two top-ranking officials I have mentioned. I note that the salary of the Auditor General is fixed by chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1931. The whole of the salary he gets is the salary set out in and determined by that statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: What is the amount of the salary?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING TENURE OF OFFICE AND SALARIES OF COMMISSIONERS
speechtext: That is 1931. That salary was fixed by statute in 1931.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Well, is it not still the same salary that was fixed by statute? Although I have looked at it fairly closely, for all I know it may be that in the financial administration act there is some provision to change the salary of the Auditor General. If it is being changed in that way, then at least that is the proper way to change it.
I was about to point out that the salary of the chief electoral officer is also fixed by statute, namely chapter 46 of the statutes of 1938, as amended. And, to anticipate the question of the Minister of Public Works, I may say that his salary is $10,000 a year.
Up to the present time the principle that the salary of the civil service commissioners should be set by statute has been recognized by the fact that their salaries were fixed by chapter 53 of the statutes of 1947. Apparently the government has taken the view for a number of years that the salaries fixed for the commissioners by that statute were not sufficient. So for a number of years they have had a special estimate providing for a supplement of $2,000 a year. As I have already isaid, the Auditor General has commented unfavourably on the practice of continuing to pay supplements in respect of salaries in that way, and has suggested that the appropriate statute should be amended. But instead of taking the Auditor General's advice, which has been advocated from the floor of the house many times, the government is taking this further step of taking away from parliament altogether the fixing of the salaries of the civil service commissioners.
