subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the house is aware, since this bill was given second reading it has been reviewed by the special committee of the house on radio broadcasting. As tonight the house will be reviewing the bill, it may be that the discussion will be somewhat broken up in order to relate it to the particular sections. At the outset, Mr. Chairman, I might say that the special committee has completed its public sittings but has not yet written its report, so the discussion tonight is necessarily in advance of the writing of the report, let alone its tabling in the house. However, having regard to the rather advanced stage of this session, I suppose it will be too much to expect that there will be an opportunity for discussing the report of the special committee when it is tabled.
I feel it is unfortunate that the bill should be before the house before we actually have the report of the special committee. I am sure we would have had a more concentrated and more helpful discussion if the house had the advantage of having before it the report of the special committee.
May I say this in general about the meetings of the committee. I think all members who were present will agree that the meetings were instructive. We had the assistance of the senior officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and questioned them freely. They gave us a good deal of information. The committee also had assistance from representatives of the Canadian association of broadcasters, representing the great majority of the private broadcasting stations in Canada. They gave their views on a broad range of subjects, and were very appropriately thanked by the committee for their helpful presentation. The committee also spent a day in Montreal examining the Radio Canada building, and seeing some demonstrations of television which were indeed interesting to all members present. In other words, the sittings of the committee, Mr. Chairman, were helpful to all concerned, and I think the committee has performed a service to the house and to the country.
The relationships between this committee and the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have always been very cordial. Even those who disagreed with the policy of the broadcasting corporation on some of the matters in which policy has played a leading part have always been glad and happy in the association of the committee and those senior officials.
The subject of programs did provide a source of some agitation in the committee
Canadian Broadcasting Act meetings this year. I do not want to discuss that subject, in detail in advance of the writing of the committee's report. I believe the report may have something to say on that subject this year. But I feel that all hon. members of this house should do two things in expressing their views on the subject of programs. First of all we should vindicate the principle of freedom of expression. Some representations are being made through the mails these days to members of the house that seem to suggest some people are becoming very panicky, and believe there is some effort afoot to interfere with legitimate freedom of expression on the air. I do not believe anyone in this house is going to suggest there should be any tampering or interference with the established principle of freedom of expression. On the other hpnd, as applied to this vitally important means of communication, we must have regard at all times, and particularly when the control of radio broadcasting in Canada is vested in a publicly owned and appointed board of governors, to the necessity of providing balance in the presentation of points of view.
Much of the criticism that has been levelled at certain programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation might well have been avoided if the corporation, instead of making a series of broadcasts by persons having a particular point of view, had sought at the same time to provide balance in the presentation of that point of view by giving equal opportunity on the same series to those who had a different point of view to express. It seems to me that those who are charged under the present set-up with the control of broadcasting in Canada, not only on the channels occupied by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation but on others which are after all under residual control of that corporation, should take great care to see that due respect is paid to the fundamental convictions of the people of this country. We heard that certain programs offended the religious sensibilities of people in Canada. We heard criticism of other programs because in a political sense they leaned too much to one particular point of view.
Recognizing the difficulty, and asserting at all times that the principle of freedom must be vindicated, we must nevertheless insist, in the first place, that anything in the nature of unnecessary offence to the religious and moral convictions of the people of the country must be avoided, and in the matter of programs having a political flavour, or news commentators and political commentators, a balance must be preserved. There is one situation that has been discussed more than once-I mention this because it struck some of us very
i 846

Canadian Broadcasting Act forcibly at the time-concerning the series of political commentators under the title "Capital Report". When it came to totalling the number of those who participated in that particular series, that element of balance was not found present which the board of governors subscribes to, we are told, as a principle. There was criticism of this series which I for one voiced in the committee because those participating in it were, on the whole, leftist in their tendencies. That was the flavour of the reports. When we came to get the figures of those participating we found that out of 41 broadcasts in that iseries 28 had been delivered by one individual, Matthew Halton. Mr. Halton is an accomplished commentator; but in the opinion of most people I think his political views and comments are somewhat left of centre. When we come to examine the the other participants in that series, thinking in terms of balance, we find that Mr. Robert McKenzie had two; Milton Shulman, 3; Elmore Philpott, 3; Herbert Steinhouse, 3; Gerard Fay, 1; Jon Kimche, 1; Andrew Cowan, 1; Douglas Lachance, 1; Peter Stursberg, 1. When that matter was brought directly to the attention of the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation he readily agreed that it did not represent balance in a series where the point of view of the commentator is of no little importance. I am glad to say the chairman said that the unbalance in that particular series would be redressed.
I do not propose to repeat what was said three weeks ago in the debate on second reading of this bill. The subject of the fundamental method of control of radio broadcasting in Canada has been before the house on more than one occasion. This bill does not present an opportunity of seeking a test of opinion in the house on that subject because there is no one section that provides a vehicle for testing that opinion thereon. One must therefore content oneself at this stage with one or two general observations.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation strongly supports the present system of broadcasting in Canada, under which control of all broadcasting is vested in the board of governors. The Canadian association of broadcasters, on the other hand, took the position that there should be an independent regulatory tribunal which would have controlling powers so far as may be necessary to preserve freedom on the airwaves. Their contention was that there is no necessity for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to sit in judgment upon them.
We must never lose sight of the fact that radio broadcasting has become a highly competitive business. We have an abundance


of evidence to show that as between private broadcasting stations in similar localities or in the same localities competition is exceedingly keen. As between private stations on the one hand and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the other, competition operates so far as is permitted by the corporation, and that competition is keen. The problem therefore is inescapable: is it right and fair that in that area in which keen competition exists, the system of control and regulation should be such that one of the competitors exercises control over the whole field, including its competitors? That is the problem.
. To meet that problem Dr. Arthur Surveyer, one of the members of the Massey commission, put forward some concrete proposals which I am bound to say commend themselves strongly to some of us. They are not exactly the views put forward on that subject by the Canadian association of broadcasters, but Dr. Surveyer put forward on that subject views which I wish there were an opportunity of testing effectively in the house, so hon. members might determine whether the house can disregard those views and pass them by. His view was that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should carry on as an operating body, that the board of governors should be reduced in size, and that there should be established by act of parliament a separate tribunal which would exercise regulatory power over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private stations alike, in so far as regulation may be necessary. As the matter of the licensing of stations is extremely important, it would necessarily follow that the body to advise the Minister of Transport, who issues the licenses for transmitting stations, should not be the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation but should be this independent regulatory body.
We have not before us the report of the committee. We simply have those two points of view put before the committee. While they do not exactly correspond to the majority and minority reports of the Massey commission, nevertheless there is some resemblance to those reports in the views expressed on the one hand, by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation officials and, on the other hand, by the representatives of the Canadian association of broadcasters. For my own part, Mr. Chairman, I wish to express clearly my view that the recommendations of the minority report of Dr. Arthur Surveyer, a Montreal engineer of high distinction, contain a sensible proposal for handling this problem of the regulation of broadcasting in Canada.

Then, sir, there is one other subject, namely television, which I should like to mention on this opening section. What I have to say with regard to the method of financing the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I shall reserve for section 6 of the bill. The subject of television 'is of striking importance. We are told that there are some 60,000 television receiving sets in Canada. These receiving sets are today receiving United States programs. They are located within reach of the border. There is today no Canadian television. Why is there not? The answer is that it was policy on the part of the government-policy which agreed with the views of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation- that there should not be Canadian television hitherto. On the one hand, when private applicants came forward and, as long ago as early 1948, made application for television licenses, those applications were simply held in a state of suspense. There are four such applications pending for two available channels in Toronto. There are two applications pending for three available channels in Montreal. There are applications pending in Hamilton, Winnipeg, New Westminster and several other Canadian cities. With the exception of one application from Hamilton which was dismissed, the others, for periods running up to almost four years, have been held simply in a state of suspense. Why? Because it was government policy, as well as policy of the board of governors of the corporation, that no private television be hitherto permitted in Canada.
What has the corporation done as regards television itself? Well, after a slow start, for which I think the government is principally responsible rather than the corporation, the corporation has been pressing its efforts to provide television over two channels assigned to them, one in Toronto and one in Montreal. When the committee of the 1950 session reviewed this matter, it was told by the officials of the corporation it was their hope and expectation that television programs would be available from these two stations by September last. It is a matter of disappointment to all concerned, including the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, that shortages of materials and delays arising out of that fact have defeated that hope. Now the earliest date by which the officials of the corporation hold out any hope of television over these two stations is the summer of 1952, and apparently there is some uncertainty as to whether television may be expected even then.
The first stage of development contemplates that television will be provided over these
Canadian Broadcasting Act two stations. There will in time be connections between Toronto and Montreal. There will be a network; there will be provision for relays and kinescope recordings, and efforts of that kind. The whole undertaking in this first stage will cost approximately $5,225,000, and will require at least a couple of years to complete.
What of the other areas in Canada which are unquestionably just as anxious to have Canadian television programs made available to them as the more fortunate people of Montreal and Toronto? That depends on the second stage of development, Mr. Chairman. Some effort will be made in the first stage to provide by kinescope recordings television in some of the other principal cities. For transmission of television from stations in those other principal cities in Canada they may have to wait for some considerable time, and the cost is going to be very great. We were told in the committee on Monday that the cost to complete this second stage may well run to something like $15 million; and there will be required, in addition to what has now been provided1 by parliament over and above commercial revenues from the sale of sponsored programs, $10 million during the first four years of operation.
Now, sir, these are the plans of the national system. I have indicated that the government is to be held responsible for the fact that these plans have been held back, and that today we are still without Canadian television in this country. One does not underestimate the difficulties. This is a new field, and I want to be quite fair in my approach to it. There are very great difficulties involved in television, in launching this new form of communication.
The plans of the corporation do not contemplate, even at the beginning, operations for more than perhaps three hours a day on these two stations. It will take a good deal of time to develop programs, to develop engineering and program techniques, to the point where Canadians will be able to have sustained enjoyment of television programs. In the face of all that, and the responsibility the government must bear for holding back the development of television under other auspices, as well as delay in the early stages of the development of television by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself, one asks how the government hopes to justify denying entry into this field to those who are quite prepared to come in and take their chances.
It is not enough, surely, for the government to take a paternalistic attitude and

Canadian Broadcasting Act say: Well, we do not want to see you risk your money. These people are quite prepared to come in and run the risks-and they are very great risks-of losing money in the early stages of television. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation expects in the early stages of its operations to incur substantial expenditures; and those who made application for television licences well knew that for a period of time they might incur very heavy losses. But, sir, they were quite prepared to do it. In the face of their willingness to pioneer in this field, to take their chances and provide programs, it was the policy of this government to close and bolt the door, and to deny to any private interests any opportunity of entry into this field. What is the result? These dozen or more applications are still in a state of suspense.
The majority on the Massey commission made some recommendations on this subject that I for one cannot support. At page 303 they set forth this, among other recommendations:
c. That no private television broadcasting stations be licensed until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has available national television programs and that all private stations be required to serve as outlets for national programs.
That recommendation, literally applied, will mean that until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has brought into effect stage one of its television plans, which will not even commence until at least next summer, no consideration will be given to any of these applications for television licences. They are still to be left in a state of suspense. Moreover, sir, let me remind you that the opening of broadcasting from Toronto and Montreal simply marks the opening of stage one of the television plans of the corporation, and it may be another couple of years before stage one is fully put into operation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That leaves us with this unhappy consequence: that apparently it will be two or three years before any consideration is to be given these pending applications. In the meantime the door is closed to anybody else in Canada wanting to enter this field. It means that because the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is encountering delays-there are shortages of different kinds now and their plans will have to be proceeded with under the limitations of finance-Canadians are not going to have much television in this country for at least several years to come, and they will not have television on any very substantial scale for apparently a great many years to come. And this is government policy.
It is the government that, through the Minister of Transport, issues the licences. The

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation advises the minister with regard to the issuance of those licences. The policy in these matters or views on policy are shared by the government and the board of governors of the corporation. Apparently they see eye to eye, and I for one say it is most regrettable that Canadians are to be denied television.
Let us not be turned aside, sir, by any talk about undue commercialism or an excess of United States content in these programs, because, sir, the content of programs is still subject to the regulatory powers of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, No one has ever suggested in this House of Commons, so far as I am aware, that there should not be regulation exercised over television, as over sound broadcasting. There is going to be some form of regulation, whether it be carried on by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or by some independent regulatory board or tribunal. Therefore that regulatory tribunal, whatever it may be-and under the present system it would be the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself-would have ample power to see that there is not an undue commercial content in any television programs sent out from private stations, and also that there was not any undue American content. All of us want to see as high a content of Canadian broadcasting in Canadian television as may be in keeping with good programs. It will take time to develop Canadian television talent and Canadian television techniques. But valuable time is being lost and unfairness is being perpetrated by the government, not simply on people who are applying for licences but upon the people who want to receive television.
Meantime, because of the concentration of television in these two major urban centres in Canada, Montreal and Toronto, the benefits of television, in so far as it is developed, are going to be enjoyed largely by the residents of these two great urban centres.
The government has not yet told us very much about how television is to be financed. The chairman of the board of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation indicated in his evidence last Monday that a receiving licence fee of $15 is probably going to be required, to make up the very large gap between revenues and expenditures of the corporation in television. Already the house has authorized substantial loans to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the development of television. Speaking from memory, these loans already aggregate $4,500,000. I think it will be a matter of concern to all members that, when these substantial expenditures have been authorized out of public

moneys, the benefits of television in Canada should be as widely diffused as possible. It seems to me that that healthy diffusion of the benefits of television will be defeated by this policy of concentrating the development of television exclusively in the hands of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and denying to all others any opportunity of participating in that development.
These are only a few of the matters which have come before the committee. I wish it were possible for the opinion of the house to be tested on those two very important subjects which I have sought to discuss tonight. The first of these is:	What type of
regulatory machinery should be set up in Canada? Should it be an independent body standing apart from both the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its competitors among the private stations; or should it be the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself which, to a large extent, is a competitor of many of these private stations?
The other question is this:	Should the
development of television be hampered in the way the government is hampering it today? Why should not Canadians be permitted by the government to enjoy the benefits of television? There should be an opportunity of testing the opinion of the house with regard to that government policy. Unfortunately this bill does not offer adequate opportunity in that regard. But some day, and I hope before long, I am sure an effective opportunity will be given to the Canadian parliament to express its verdict upon that barren, negative government policy.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to join the hon. member for Eglinton in saying how enjoyable the meetings of the radio committee have been, not only this year but in former years, and how we have appreciated the information and advice we received in that committee from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and, indeed, through the representations from time to time of the Canadian association of broadcasters, representing many of the private stations.
As one who has served on that committee almost continuously-with the exception of two-I have been interested to see how, bit by bit, the original intention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has been set aside, and to a large extent the authority of government bodies, both the Department of Transport and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, reduced.
Those of us who have been familiar for a number of years with broadcasting in this country will well recollect the establishment of the Aird commission, and we will recall
Canadian Broadcasting Act what the Aird commission recommended, because of the chaotic and unsatisfactory condition of broadcasting in Canada. The Aird commission recommended that we should have a completely government owned and controlled broadcasting system, that the private stations that existed at the time of the passing of the act which established the original Canadian Broadcasting Commission should be expropriated, and that we should have only a dominion-wide government owned publicly controlled broadcasting system in this country. That was the idea Right Hon. R. B. Bennett had when he introduced the first act governing broadcasting in Canada. I am not going to quote Mr. Bennett at this time; but When I look back over the years and recollect the warnings he gave the house, both when that act was passed and when the new act was passed in 1936, I believe it was, I realize how far-sighted he was in his prognostications of what might happen in the future.
No government we have had in Canada, whether Conservative or Liberal, since the first broadcasting legislation was introduced in 1932, has sought to change the original conception. That original conception was that, because of the peculiar nature of the country, because of its great distances, because of the scattered population, because we have two great peoples with different cultural origins, the only manner in which we could have a satisfactory system of broadcasting was to have one owned and controlled by the people through their government, and operated by a corporation set up by and operating under a statute of parliament And in 1936, when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was piloting through the house a new act, he said this:
Radio broadcasting in Canada has been studied by one royal commission and three parliamentary committees,-
That was before 1936.
-and these four reports agree on the broad principles that must govern us. That is to say, the aim of broadcasting should be complete coverage by government facilities and the present situation demands complete control over all forms of broadcasting whether public or private. These conditions are being maintained in the present bill.
Apparently the private broadcasters accepted that situation, until they made their recent representations. In those recent representations they have gone far beyond anything they ever asked before. What they actually asked for this time was the repeal of the acts as we understand and know them,
1850	HOUSE OF
Canadian Broadcasting Act the setting aside of the very basis of broadcasting in this country as we have known it hitherto. In their brief they said this:
We believe that regulations applied to broadcasting should be for only the required technical purposes so that order may be maintained on the airwaves, and that broadcasting should not be subjected to controls which do not apply to any other form of mass communication.
In other words all that this house could do, and I presume the Department of Transport under the act, would be to see to it that the airwaves were properly apportioned, that interference was looked after and all that kind of thing, and that the private stations should be in the same position as are the newspapers of Canada. What they forget of course is that they are in a different position to the newspapers of Canada because they are occupying publicly owned airwaves which are granted to them for the time being and over which during that time they exercise some control. In other words, a monopoly of an air wavelength is granted to a private organization by the government, or by the people of Canada if you like that better, as a privilege and not as a right.
When we hear about business competition in connection with broadcasting between the private organizations themselves or between the private organizations and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation it is not competition in the ordinary sense of the word because to begin with a private broadcasting station, under acts passed first by the Conservatives and then by the present government and affirmed all through the years in the reports of various parliamentary committees, is placed in a position where it is under the control of a publicly organized authority. As I say, their representations this year went far beyond anything they have asked for heretofore. I should like to refer to page 151 of the record of the proceedings of the 1947 committee. Mr. Sedgwick was appearing on behalf of the private broadcasters and on June 3, 1947, he said this:
. . . such freedom of speech should be properly safeguarded by having the regulation of radio broadcasting in the hands of a licensing and regulatory body which should be as independent as possible of the government of the day and which should be appointed directly by and responsible directly to parliament itself.
In other words in 1947, while they were asking for a different kind of regulatory body, they wanted a body to regulate all matters having to do with radio broadcasting. This year they have asked for something different. In support of the request for a new regulatory body they quote Dr. Surveyer. I wondered why they quoted Dr. Surveyer. If you will read his minority report you will find


that he does recommend a regulatory body different from the C.B.C., and why? Because he thinks the C.B.C. is too busy to undertake the proper regulation of broadcasting in Canada. He quotes at some length to prove that radio broadcasting has not carried out the function it should have carried out in raising the tastes of the Canadian people. In fact he quotes various authorities to suggest that radio broadcasting has not hastened the maturity of many of the people of Canada. He quotes a number of experts and authorities to support these contentions, and he has this to say, as found at page 398 of the report of the Massey commission:
The excerpts and quotations given above reveal what heavy responsibilities will be placed on the shoulders of the members of the independent regulating body charged with the task of not only arbitrating on the disagreements between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private broadcasters, but also with the more difficult mission of planning an adequate and well balanced schedule of radio and television programs for Canada. It is obvious that the group of men who will have this double responsibility should not be charged with this other double duty of operating the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation networks and of producing the programs suggested by the new control board.
In his recommendation for a new regulatory body I think Dr. Surveyer goes far beyond anything we in this parliament would approve or accept. He wants a regulatory body which would be responsible for raising the whole tone of Canadian broadcasting and which would, as he says, bring about a greater maturity of mind, thinking, culture and taste among the people of Canada. In other words, for the private broadcasters to call in Dr. Surveyer to support a private regulatory body-a minority report, in other words-is, I think, to destroy the very argument that some of my bon. friends are using in that connection.
I do not want to speak at any great length. The hon. member for Eglinton mentioned the criticisms that have been made of some of the programs that have been heard on the air. I am convinced that when second reading of the bill was before the house and we were discussing this matter, many hon. members who spoke had either not heard the broadcasts that were then under criticism or had not read the scripts. As it happened I had heard most of the broadcasts complained of, and I had the temerity to say in the house that I thought they were the kind of broadcast that a good many people in Canada should be entitled to hear. I was not only criticized in the house for having said that but subsequently I received a number of letters to the same effect. I think hon. members who were on the radio committee, and who have had an opportunity to read the scripts that were

the basis of the broadcasts, will agree that in the main they were in very fine language, that there was nothing of a blasphemous nature and that they were the kind of thing that is heard daily in the classrooms of our colleges.
The only suggestion I would make is one that as a matter of fact was made also by the hon. member for Eglinton. I would suggest that when topics of that type are discussed on the air by scientists or others and they come to conclusions which may not be the opinion of a majority or even a large minority of the people of Canada, at the end of that same series of broadcasts an opportunity should be given to put the other side of the case. I may say that I listen with a great deal of interest to many different types of broadcasts. I enjoy the religious programs on Sunday afternoon. Some of them are distinctly doctrinal. They speak of the doctrines of the various churches and are of great interest. I have listened to a series of broadcasts by eminent clergymen of the Roman Catholic church, my own church which is the Anglican church, the Baptist church and the Presbyterian church, on a recent Sunday evening series dealing with the development of Christian thought, and have enjoyed them very much.
I think all sides of these questions should be presented to the people of Canada in order that we may arrive at some maturity in our thought. As I say, the only proviso I would make is that where something of a very controversial nature is being discussed an opportunity should be given for someone to reply. In connection with the four-I think that is the number-broadcasts by Dr. Hoyle of Cambridge university on the nature of the universe, which have been under criticism, at the end of that series of broadcasts a Roman Catholic priest I believe from St. Michael's college in Toronto replied to the position taken by Dr. Hoyle from the religious and Christian point of view.
I think it is perfectly satisfactory when that is done. I am happy to know that the church to which I belong, the Anglican church in Canada, held a meeting of its bishops and ohancellors a short time ago who came to the unanimous conclusion that broadcasts of the type that have been under criticism should be permitted, indeed encouraged, provided that an opportunity for criticism is given. That was also the position taken by the United Church of Canada. I was interested to see that the Prairie Messenger, a paper which circulates widely in Saskatchewan and which is published by the Benedictine Fathers in that province, took a similar position in an editorial. That was the position taken by
Canadian Broadcasting Act that great and influential Roman Catholic order. The same position was taken by the Canadian council of churches.
If we are to have freedom of speech on the air opportunity must be given for the airing of views with which some of us may disagree from time to time, always provided that an opportunity is given for the making of an adequate reply. In these days when freedom of speech is so essential we must beware lest we fall into the trap of limiting the freedom of speech we now have.
I do not know the political views of some of the commentators who have been criticized, and I was surprised to hear tonight that Matthew Halton was left of centre. I have listened to him on many occasions and have always thought he was pretty objective in his remarks. As I pass across the country I have been told by Liberals, Conservatives, C.C.F.'ers, Social Crediters and people of every shade of opinion that the one commentator they have enjoyed over the years is Matthew Halton. He has been acclaimed by various broadcasting authorities, both in North America and overseas, as being one of the ablest broadcasters anywhere in the world. I do not know most of the others well enough to say much about them, although I have listened to them with a great deal of interest.
I am glad provision is to be made for the financing of the corporation. I believe that if the house approves the suggestion made as to financing more adequate programs will be available. I hope that will be so. I hope also that a greater limit will be placed on the amount of advertising over the air. I did not bring with me this evening the copy of Time of December 3 which I saw a few days ago, and which outlined the amounts spent on advertising by some of the big corporations in the United States. I remember that one was spending $43 million a year on advertising. One of the toothpaste and soap organizations was spending around $16 million a year.
People think they get their radio programs free over the private stations, but they do not. They pay for them in the soap, in the toothpaste, in the sausages, in the soup, in almost everything they buy. They pay through the nose for those things advertised on the various stations, including the private stations and those of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We would not buy some of these products at all if they were not constantly named and drummed into our ears hour after hour over the radio and constantly kept before our eyes in the various newspapers and other publications that we see. No wonder we pay 83 cents for a tube

Canadian Broadcasting Act of toothpaste that I am told costs 9 or 10 or 12 cents to make and package. We pay dearly for radio programs through advertising.
May I say a word about television. Like my hon. friend I spent a most interesting day at Montreal looking over the headquarters of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I think all Canadians can be proud of those headquarters at Montreal. I hope that with the additional funds we are proposing to appropriate through this bill the facilities in other places like Toronto, Winnipeg and elsewhere will be improved.
I repeat that we can be proud of what we saw in Montreal. We can be proud of the people who are doing the job in Montreal and across the country. There is a fine staff of young men and women who have entered this new field which has been developed over the last twenty years, and who are doing a competent and splendid job in radio broadcasting.
I think what interested us most on this visit was the television. We had the opportunity to see how far the corporation had gone in its preparations to give television to this country. I marvelled first at the intricacy of the equipment required both for radio and television. We sometimes speak of literacy as though it were merely the ability to write and perhaps develop our mental faculties in a literary way, but I sometimes feel most illiterate in another sense when I visit places of this description and see the intricate machinery and equipment with which many of these younger people have to work. It is all dutch to me, if I may put it that way. What these people are doing in Montreal is a great credit to them and to Canada.
Who is going to give us television? The hon. member for Eglinton would like to see the private stations take over television and give us presumably the kind of television they are getting in the United States. If that were done it would be a punishment upon all the people of Canada for the negligence of this House of Commons at the present time. I do not want to see our people undergo the kind of punishment they are getting in the United States from the private telecasting organizations. I have noticed statements that have appeared in certain responsible newspapers, not only those which support the government but those which ordinarily support the friends of the hon. member for Eglinton. The Ottawa Journal has the reputation of being a Conservative paper. An editorial in tonight's issue deals with a brief presented a few days ago by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in which they alleged to represent 100,000

businessmen in this country. They urged that an opportunity be given to private organizations to go into television. However, the Journal questions that statement; indeed, it makes the suggestion that if a vote were taken of those 100,000 persons it might be found that the majority would disapprove of the chamber's brief presented to the government in relation to television. I am convinced that our people would rather wait a little while than have the kind of television inflicted upon them that we find to a large extent in the United States. I believe the Massey commission was very forthright, and indeed very wise, in the recommendation it made. If one will read the sections in the Massey report at pages 301, 302 and 303, where the reasons for the recommendations are given, one finds the recommendations in these terms:
That no private television broadcasting stations be licensed until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has available national television programs and that all private stations be required to serve as outlets for national programs.
They also submitted:
That direction and control of television broadcasting in Canada continue to be vested in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
That the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation proceed with plans for the production of television programs in French and English and for national coverage by kinescope recordings or by any other practicable means.
The commission is most anxious that television shall be safeguarded. It is true that today there are a number of television sets in Canada. You find them in the Niagara peninsula, in Toronto, and other places near the United States border. I am quite sure that those who have these sets would agree with me that many of the programs emanating from the United States are third or fourth rate. In the evening a great many of the programs consist of wrestling or boxing matches which are easily televised, and indeed are televised very well. But in Canada we would like to see something a little more -I hate to use the word-cultural than that sort of thing. I should like to say that I believe we are wise to wait a while, and I do not agree with the hon. member for Eglinton in saying that this is a policy of government. I like to think of the policy with regard to radio and television as a policy of this parliament. Effective public control was the policy of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, and it was the policy of the succeeding government under Right Hon. Mr. King. No fundamental change was made. It is the policy that has been consistently pursued, no matter what government has been in power. Consequently I should like to see the hon.

members of the house take pride in this as their broadcasting system, their television system; the broadcasting system of this parliament of Canada, and not of one section of this house or of any political party.
I hope that one day we may have the country covered by television. When one sees the equipment we saw in Montreal the other day, and realizes that to put television over will cost millions, not hundreds of thousands of dollars, one can realize the difficulties. The very mobile unit which we saw on the floor costs about $100,000. When you think of all the other equipment, the cost of operation and all the rest of it, it will run into the millions of dollars. As a matter of fact we were told that it takes 40 hours of preparation and rehearsal to produce a half hour program. I believe it takes seven times as many people as are engaged in the production of a radio program. When you look at those figures you begin to realize the costliness of this operation.
If television did get into private hands the organizations that could put on television programs would have to be very wealthy indeed. If you relied on advertising only, then the wealthiest corporations in Canada would be the only ones who could afford to advertise. Resale price maintenance would be nothing to the monopoly you would create if radio advertising did take care of television, because only the most powerful nation-wide organizations who were prepared to spend millions in advertising could take advantage of those facilities. Consequently I am one of those who believe that the Massey commission was right in its recommendations that we should proceed slowly, and that we should make this a Canadian effort. We should try to provide both our English and French speaking people with television as quickly as possible, but we should take every precaution to see that television is used for entertainment, for education, but most of all to promote the consciousness of Canada, our Canadian way of life, and our Canadian culture, and not to sell this country down the river to our friends to the south.

speechtext:
Canadian Broadcasting Act
I have some criticism to offer in respect of these matters. One of the representations that has come through the mail to us makes special reference to the C.B.C. white paper with which I think we are all familiar. These representations deplore what they surmise may be some interference with this white paper. They want the principles involved in that white paper to continue and to be established. I am not going to criticize the white paper particularly, but I am going to analyse it a little and expound something which I trust will be a bit thought-provoking. This particular representation goes on to say:
According to the C.B.C. white paper on political and controversial broadcasting which has been approved by parliament in the past, the basic principles of this national policy are:
I am going to read them, and I am going to comment on them as I go along.
1.	The air belongs to the people-
May I interject here that I have some reservation with respect to that assertion. I do not know that it does belong to the people. At least I will say that phrase "it belongs to the people" is a socialist phrase. But let me read the whole section:
The air belongs to the people, who are entitled to hear the principal points of view on all questions of importance.
The question I want to ask here is this. Who is to determine what the principal points of view are, and who is to determine what the questions of importance are? Another thing I am going to suggest is this. If the air belongs to the people, and if they are entitled to hear the principal points of view on all questions of importance, I am going to ask this question: Are they entitled to hear it at the taxpayers' expense?
2.	The air must not fall under the control of any individuals or groups influential by reason of their wealth or special position.
I want to emphasize the last words "or special position" because the air does fall under the control of individuals with special position. It falls under the control of the talks department which is composed of people who are in a special position, for they are the ones who formulate the programs and decide on the people who must take part in opinion broadcasts.
3.	The right to answer is inherent in the democratic doctrine of free speech.
I believe that; but we have not the right to answer over the national networks in this *country. Someone has a right only if that someone is chosen by those in a special position and he is asked: Would you mind giving this series a little balance? Will you, along with others, take part in this series of talks?
[Mr. Hansell.l

I am saying that the right to answer'which is inherent in the democratic doctrine of free speech is not a principle that is being followed in the 'opinion broadcasts on our national networks.
I now come to another thing:
4.	Freedom of speech and the full interchange of opinion are among the principal safeguards of free institutions.
Once again I am going to say that there is no full interchange of opinion. It is only as full as the talks department care to make it. I know that it is not just the easiest thing in the world to arrange, and I am not harshly criticizing those four principles, because I recognize the fact that you have to put in there something to guide those who are in the special position of being able to say who is to take part in opinion broadcasts.
I now want to say just a word or two with respect to the particular series of broadcasts that have come in for some considerable criticism, and I am happy that this is so. I believe the officials of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should also be glad, because that is the only way they are able to know what the people are thinking about. I want to say one thing. In my opinion- and it may differ from that of a good many- the broadcasts that were given in that particular series were anti-Christian. I am not wanting to cast any reflection upon the individuals who gave them. They may be good men and honest men. They may be speaking their own personal convictions. But in my opinion they ran contrary to what I would regard as being in the best interests of our Christian way of life. Surely we can put down as one great solid factor that the foundation upon which any nation can be built and made great is the foundation of Christian principles. Surely we can put that down as one solid, indisputable fact. Surely we want to build a great nation of God-fearing people. Surely we want to build a great nation whose people will recognize our dependence upon almighty God, the Creator and the Redeemer of men and of nations. Surely we want to do that. Very well, then. "If the foundations be destroyed, what will the righteous do?" That last phrase is a quotation from holy writ. Therefore I say that even though we may desire to have a properly balanced program of opinion broadcasts, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be very careful lest that institution be used to ultimately destroy the foundations upon which any great nation is built, the foundations which will make any nation great.
I wonder whether I might just refer to one or two of these broadcasts in question.

I am going to take the broadcast given by Dr. Brock Chisholm. I know what is going to be said. It is said all the time, as soon as you mention somebody's name. "Oh, well, now, you are going to slur some character; you are going to do this, you are going to do that. Let us not bring personalities into this thing." That is the cry that goes up. Let me say to you, Mr. Chairman, that any man who enters public life opens himself to public criticism. Some of us know that. I am going to say right now that no election campaign has ever been fought where public men, in some phase or another, have not been attacked. That is the natural process, because men in public life are responsible to the public and express themselves, or have opinions that are in the interests of, or in the disinterest of, the public; we can expect criticism.
I have never met Dr. Chisholm. I suppose he is a charming gentleman, a good man, a good citizen. I am not disparaging the person at all, but I am going to read one or two things he said in his broadcast. I cannot take time to quote too much. The broadcast, to start with, has as its theme "Man's last enemy, himself." He starts off in the introductory remarks with a very familiar quotation, "Man, know thyself." His broadcast is designed to bring to his listeners the important theme that man must know himself. Very well. Who is to teach man himself? Who is to teach man what he is? Who is to teach man so that man can know himself? We do not read very far in the broadcast until we come to the point which he illustrates, namely that if anything goes wrong with the washing machine, or the refrigerator does not work properly, you call in an expert to do whatever needs to be done. He goes on to say that the same principle is involved in this theme. Therefore if you want to know yourself you have to bring in the experts. He never tells us who the experts are; oh, no. I should like to know who they are. Perhaps he regards himself as one, and I have no quarrel with him if he does, but I am going to say this. I will tell you who I think the experts are. He deals with the matter of child psychology. The greatest experts in the world are the Christian mothers and fathers who bring up their children in the admonition of almighty God. They are the experts. Give me the kind of parents who will bring up their children in Christian teaching, with the devotion and affeotion those parents give to children; give me those, and I will put them alongside the Chisholms, the Freuds and the Camerons, or anyone of their kind, and I will guarantee that the nation will be stronger. The nations
Canadian Broadcasting Act of the world will be stronger if we pay a little more attention to these kinds of experts.
What do the experts say, after all? I will tell you. They say: "Come along here. You are a man. I am going to teach you to know yourself. I will take your brain and put it on the table, and I will begin to dissect it. I will take your personality, and I will tell you all about your personality. I will dissect that, too. If you want to give me your gizzard) I will put that on the table, and I will begin to dissect that, too. And after I have them all dissected I will put them back again and I will make a new man out of you, so that after I get through you will be able to understand yourself." That is just about the way they work. Well, by the time I got through reading this broadcast I made a little note on the bottom, and that little note in my handwriting is this: "I don't know myself any better than I did before I read the broadcast."
Let me go on a little further, Mr. Chairman. I notice that it is nearly ten o'clock, but if I may just have a few more minutes I will be through.

There is another part in this broadcast that I do not like, and I should like to mention it. Dr. Chisholm refers to certain things, and he gives an illustration. He is talking about the rate of increase in world population, and he says it has jumped to about 68,000 a day. He then asks this question:
Are you among the hundreds of millions of people who are avoiding this frightening fact? Are you among those whose opinion, based on some authoritarian prejudice, prevents delegates to the United Nations bodies, even the population commission, from tackling this problem?
That leaves it in the air. Who is this prejudiced authoritarian who seeks to channel and control men's opinions? He does not say. Perhaps I know to whom he refers, but I do say that to put that in a broadcast and pour it into the ears of several million people is not fair. There are some people in the world who, because of their Christian concepts, have a great deal of respect for those who are in religious authority, and I believe that such phraseology is just taking advantage of them.
I might go on. He spends a good deal of time giving illustrations about the way parents should teach their children in respect of their bowel movements. I am not going to have anything to say about that, but once again I am saying that I do not think you can teach a mother and father very much about their children in that respect. He

Canadian Broadcasting Act goes on to show how you can approach it from an angle which will have a particular reaction upon the child after he grows up. You can take that for what it is worth. I do not think it is worth very much. Then he goes on in his broadcast to talk about a child's sexual equipment. Well, some may smile. Some may say, "Why bring that up in parliament?" All I am going to say is: Why pour it into the ears of a few million people?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
We believe in free speech. We like free speech. But let us not run away with the notion that the only place we can have free speech is over the radio networks of Canada. We are told the air belongs to the people. Well, it belongs only as far as one's voice will carry, and always has. We have no objection to a man gathering a few people around him, if he has an idea he would like to propound. There is nothing to prevent that idea from taking hold. There is nothing to prevent those people saying, "It is good; we think you should expound it further. We will call in a few more of our friends."
There is nothing to prevent a man from gathering a few supporters around him. That is not very difficult. And if his idea is worth anything it is not difficult for him to get on the air, even though in a small way. His friends will support him. He can start out on a small station at very small expense, and give voice to his idea.
That is free speech. And if it catches on, then some other stations will want it. Eventually the idea will become well known, but he does not have to express his ideas at the

expense of the taxpayers. Almost anyone can get on the air in a small way if he has something worthwhile to say.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext: Did you hear Mr. Fair last night?.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE NUMBER OF GOVERNORS, PROVIDE PENSIONS AND FURTHER GRANTS
speechtext:
We must not think the only place free speech can be expressed is over a national network. I do not know whether those in this series of broadcasts who have been criticized take that view or not. If the psychiatrists have an idea, let them gather their friends around them. Let them pay for some time on a private station. Then if the idea catches on, let it spread. Someone will want it, in that event. But they should not do it at the taxpayers' expense.
But some of these people look at it differently and will say, "Oh, no; this is different. Here is a multimillion dollar corporation with huge networks capable of reaching millions of people. Why not take advantage of it?" I do not think I am far off the beam when I say the attitude is, "Well, if you pull the right wire, know the right people, and go about it in the right way, eventually you may get on the national networks, at the expense of the taxpayers, and be paid for doing it." That is the way it works.
I do not think I need say anything further. I could go on criticizing all these speeches, but I will reserve what I have to say until we reach other sections of the bill. There are one or two other matters about which I shall have something to say. I have set out my objections, and perhaps what I have said will be accepted as a contribution to the discussion.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue the consideration of Bill No. 17, to amend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936; and then a list of small bills: Bill No. 41, to amend the Dominion Elections Act; Bill No. 42, to amend the National Gallery Act; Bill No. 43, to amend the Civil Service Act; Bill No. 8, to amend the North Fraser Harbour Commissioners Act; Bill No. 18, to provide for the establishment of an agricultural products board; the resolution in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning the provision for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces and, if we have time, Bill No. 23, to amend the Government Annuities Act.
